subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — KS3
ask: Which part of a cell controls what it does and holds the DNA?
why: The nucleus holds the chromosomes, and the chromosomes carry the instructions for every protein the cell can make — so it controls the cell by controlling what gets built.
choices: Nucleus|Cell membrane|Cytoplasm|Mitochondria

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — KS3
ask: Name one part a plant cell has that an animal cell does not.
why: A plant cell has three an animal cell has not: a cellulose cell wall for support, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a permanent vacuole holding sap.

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — KS3
ask: What is the job of the cell membrane?
why: The membrane is partially permeable — small molecules like oxygen and water pass through it, larger ones do not. That selectivity is what keeps the inside different from the outside.
choices: It controls what enters and leaves the cell|It makes food for the cell|It holds the cell’s DNA|It releases energy from glucose
answer: It controls what enters and leaves the cell

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — KS3
ask: Which cell part releases energy from glucose in respiration?
why: Aerobic respiration happens inside mitochondria, so a cell that needs a lot of energy — a muscle cell, a sperm cell — has a lot of them.
choices: Mitochondria|Ribosomes|Nucleus|Cell wall

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — KS3
ask: A red blood cell has no nucleus. Why is that useful?
why: A red blood cell is a carrying bag. Losing the nucleus frees space for more haemoglobin — and the cost is that it cannot divide or repair itself, which is why they only last about four months.
choices: It leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen|It makes the cell float|It stops the cell respiring|It lets the cell divide faster
answer: It leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which of these is a prokaryotic cell?
why: Prokaryotic means the DNA is not inside a nucleus — a bacterium has a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm, plus small rings called plasmids. Everything else on that list is eukaryotic.
choices: A bacterial cell|A plant cell|An animal cell|A fungal cell

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is diffusion?
why: Particles move randomly, so more of them happen to wander out of a crowded region than into it. Nothing pushes them — the net movement is just the odds, which is why diffusion needs no energy.
choices: The spreading of particles from high concentration to low concentration|The movement of water through a partially permeable membrane|The movement of particles against a concentration gradient|The splitting of a cell into two
answer: The spreading of particles from high concentration to low concentration

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Osmosis is the movement of which substance?
why: Osmosis is diffusion of water only, through a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a concentrated one.

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Foundation
ask: A cell is 0.05 mm long and its image is 50 mm long. What is the magnification?
why: Magnification = image ÷ real size, and both must be in the same units. 50 ÷ 0.05 = 1000.

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Foundation
ask: How many daughter cells does one cell produce by mitosis?
why: The chromosomes are copied first and then one full set is pulled to each end, so both daughters get the same DNA. Mitosis is for growth and repair; it is meiosis that makes four different cells.
choices: Two, genetically identical|Four, genetically identical|Two, genetically different|Four, genetically different

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Higher
ask: An image is 30 mm wide at ×1500. What is the real width in micrometres?
why: Real = image ÷ magnification = 30 ÷ 1500 = 0.02 mm. One millimetre is 1000 µm, so 0.02 mm is 20 µm.
choices: 20 µm|2 µm|200 µm|45 µm

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Higher
ask: Active transport differs from diffusion because it...
why: Going against the gradient is going against the odds, so something has to pay — ATP from respiration. That is why root hair cells, which take up minerals from very dilute soil water, are packed with mitochondria.
choices: moves substances against the concentration gradient and needs energy|moves substances down the concentration gradient and needs energy|moves only water molecules|happens only in plant cells
answer: moves substances against the concentration gradient and needs energy

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Higher
ask: Which stem cells can become ANY type of cell?
why: Embryonic stem cells are unspecialised and can differentiate into every cell type. Adult stem cells are more limited — bone marrow ones mainly form blood cells.
choices: Embryonic stem cells|Adult stem cells from bone marrow|Meristem cells in a leaf|Nerve cells

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Higher
ask: In which part of the cell cycle are the chromosomes copied?
why: A cell spends most of the cycle in interphase, growing, copying its DNA and making extra sub-cellular structures. Mitosis is only the separating.
choices: Before mitosis, during interphase|During mitosis itself|After the cell has divided|During cytokinesis

subject: Biology
name: Cell Biology — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a large organism need an exchange surface rather than relying on diffusion across its outer surface?
why: Volume grows faster than surface area as a thing gets bigger, so the outside cannot supply the inside. Lungs, gills and villi are all the same fix: fold the surface until the ratio works again.
choices: Its surface area to volume ratio is too small|Its surface area to volume ratio is too large|Diffusion does not happen in large organisms|Its cells do not respire
answer: Its surface area to volume ratio is too small

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — KS3
ask: Put these in order from smallest to largest: organ, cell, tissue, organ system.
why: Cells of one type group into a tissue, tissues group into an organ, organs working together make a system. Each level is built from the one below it.
choices: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system|Cell, organ, tissue, organ system|Tissue, cell, organ, organ system|Cell, tissue, organ system, organ

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — KS3
ask: Which organ system carries oxygen around the body?
why: The heart pumps blood through vessels, and the red blood cells in it carry oxygen from the lungs to every respiring cell.
choices: The circulatory system|The digestive system|The nervous system|The skeletal system

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — KS3
ask: Where is most food absorbed into the blood?
why: The small intestine is lined with villi — tiny folds that give it an enormous surface area, so digested food passes into the blood quickly.
choices: The small intestine|The stomach|The large intestine|The mouth

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — KS3
ask: What do we call a substance that speeds up a reaction in the body without being used up?
why: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They are proteins, and they are not used up — one enzyme molecule can work on thousands of substrate molecules.

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — KS3
ask: Which of these is an organ?
why: An organ is several tissues working together for one job. The heart is muscle tissue, nerve tissue and blood vessels together — one level above a tissue, one below a system.
choices: The heart|Muscle tissue|A red blood cell|The circulatory system

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which enzyme breaks down starch?
why: Amylase is a carbohydrase and turns starch into maltose and then glucose. It is made in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine.
choices: Amylase|Protease|Lipase|Catalase

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Foundation
ask: What does lipase break lipids down into?
why: A lipid is a glycerol molecule with three fatty acid chains attached, so breaking it apart gives exactly those two products back.
choices: Fatty acids and glycerol|Amino acids|Glucose|Simple sugars

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the job of bile?
why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. Emulsifying means breaking fat into droplets — more surface area for lipase to work on, so digestion is faster. Bile is not an enzyme.
choices: It neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat|It digests protein into amino acids|It absorbs glucose into the blood|It breaks starch into sugar
answer: It neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which blood vessel carries blood AWAY from the heart?
why: Arteries carry blood away — the clue is the A. They have thick muscular walls because the blood leaving the heart is at high pressure. Veins carry it back.

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the whole body?
why: The left ventricle has the thickest muscular wall of the four chambers, because it has to push blood all the way round the body. The right ventricle only reaches the lungs.
choices: The left ventricle|The right ventricle|The left atrium|The right atrium

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does an enzyme stop working when it is heated too far?
why: Heat breaks the bonds holding the protein folded. The active site is a shape, so once the shape has gone the enzyme is denatured — and unlike cooling, that does not reverse.
choices: Its active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits|It is used up by the reaction|It turns into a different enzyme|The substrate evaporates
answer: Its active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Higher
ask: An enzyme works fastest at pH 2. Where in the body is it most likely to be found?
why: The stomach makes hydrochloric acid, so its enzyme — protease, called pepsin — has an optimum around pH 2. The small intestine is alkaline, so its enzymes peak near pH 8.
choices: The stomach|The small intestine|The mouth|The liver

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Higher
ask: Coronary heart disease is caused by...
why: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself. Narrow them and the muscle gets less oxygen, so it respires less and can eventually die — which is a heart attack. A stent widens them; a statin slows the build-up.
choices: fatty material building up in the coronary arteries|a faulty heart valve leaking|too few red blood cells|the heart beating irregularly
answer: fatty material building up in the coronary arteries

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Higher
ask: Give one advantage of a mechanical heart valve over a biological one.
why: Mechanical valves last decades but the patient must take anti-clotting drugs for life, because blood clots on the artificial surface. Biological valves need no such drugs and wear out in about 12–15 years — the trade-off is the whole decision.
choices: It lasts much longer|It needs no drugs afterwards|It is quieter|It grows with the patient

subject: Biology
name: Organisation — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the name for the volume of blood the heart pumps in one minute?
why: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. Stroke volume is one beat; the rate is beats per minute; multiply them and you have a minute’s worth.
choices: Cardiac output|Stroke volume|Heart rate|Blood pressure

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — KS3
ask: What is a pathogen?
why: Pathogen just means disease-causer. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists can all be pathogens — most microorganisms are harmless or useful.
choices: A microorganism that causes disease|A type of white blood cell|A medicine that kills bacteria|A chemical made by the liver

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — KS3
ask: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
why: Measles is viral. Salmonella is a bacterium, athlete’s foot is a fungus and malaria is a protist — four different kinds of pathogen, one for each on that list.
choices: Measles|Salmonella food poisoning|Athlete’s foot|Malaria

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — KS3
ask: Name one way your body stops pathogens getting in before they reach your blood.
why: These are the barriers, and they work before any immune response: unbroken skin, mucus and cilia in the airway, stomach acid, and tears carrying an enzyme that kills bacteria.

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — KS3
ask: Which blood cells fight infection?
why: White blood cells engulf pathogens, make antibodies and make antitoxins. Red cells carry oxygen, platelets clot and plasma is the liquid that carries everything.
choices: White blood cells|Red blood cells|Platelets|Plasma

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — KS3
ask: Why should you finish a course of antibiotics even when you feel better?
why: Feeling better means most bacteria are dead, not all. The survivors are the hardiest, and letting exactly those breed is how a resistant strain gets started.
choices: Some bacteria may survive and could become resistant|The tablets go off if you keep them|Antibiotics stop working against viruses|It makes the infection last longer
answer: Some bacteria may survive and could become resistant

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Antibiotics are used to treat...
why: A virus reproduces inside your own cells, so a drug that killed it would have to damage them too. That is why there is no antibiotic for a cold — and why prescribing one does nothing but breed resistance.
choices: bacterial infections only|viral infections only|both bacterial and viral infections|fungal infections only

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: How does a vaccine make you immune?
why: The dead pathogen still carries its antigens, so the body practises on something that cannot make you ill. Memory cells stay behind, so the real infection meets a response that is already fast.
choices: A small amount of dead or inactive pathogen makes white blood cells produce antibodies|It kills every pathogen already in the body|It gives you antibodies made by someone else|It stops pathogens entering the body
answer: A small amount of dead or inactive pathogen makes white blood cells produce antibodies

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which pathogen causes malaria?
why: Malaria is a protist spread by mosquitoes, which act as the vector. Stopping the mosquito — nets, draining standing water — is as much a control as any drug.
choices: A protist|A bacterium|A virus|A fungus

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the name of the plant disease that causes patches of discoloured leaves and is caused by a virus?
why: TMV gives a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration. Less chlorophyll means less photosynthesis, so the plant grows badly.

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Where was the antibiotic penicillin first discovered?
why: Alexander Fleming noticed Penicillium mould had killed the bacteria around it. Aspirin came from willow and digitalis from foxgloves — most drugs started in a living thing.
choices: In mould growing on a culture plate|In the bark of a willow tree|In foxglove leaves|In sea water
answer: In mould growing on a culture plate

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: How are monoclonal antibodies produced?
why: The lymphocyte makes the one antibody you want but will not divide; the tumour cell divides endlessly but makes nothing useful. The hybridoma does both, so you get an unlimited supply of a single specific antibody.
choices: A mouse lymphocyte is fused with a tumour cell to make a hybridoma|They are extracted from donated blood|Bacteria are genetically modified to make them|They are made by dissolving a pathogen in acid
answer: A mouse lymphocyte is fused with a tumour cell to make a hybridoma

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: Why are monoclonal antibodies useful for targeting cancer cells?
why: Specificity is the whole point — a drug or radioactive marker carried by the antibody is delivered to the cancer cell and not to healthy ones. In practice they have caused more side effects than expected, which is why they are less widely used than hoped.
choices: They bind only to a specific antigen found on the cancer cell|They dissolve any cell they touch|They make the cancer cell divide more slowly on contact|They are absorbed only by fast-growing tissue
answer: They bind only to a specific antigen found on the cancer cell

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: In the first stage of testing a new drug, what is it tested on?
why: Preclinical testing checks toxicity and efficacy before any human is exposed. Only then do healthy volunteers get very low doses, and only then do patients get it in a clinical trial.
choices: Cells, tissues and live animals|Healthy human volunteers|Patients with the disease|Computer models only

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: What is a double-blind trial?
why: If the doctor knows, their expectations can change how they assess the patient without anyone intending it. Blinding both sides is what stops the result being a measurement of what everybody hoped for.
choices: Neither the patient nor the doctor knows who has the placebo|The patient does not know, but the doctor does|Nobody records the results until the end|The drug is tested twice on the same person
answer: Neither the patient nor the doctor knows who has the placebo

subject: Biology
name: Infection & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: A plant is short of magnesium ions. What visible symptom would you expect?
why: Magnesium sits at the centre of a chlorophyll molecule, so no magnesium means no green pigment — chlorosis. Nitrate deficiency is the other one: nitrate is needed for amino acids, so the plant is stunted rather than yellow.
choices: Yellow leaves, because it cannot make chlorophyll|Stunted growth, because it cannot make protein|Spots of mould on the leaves|Holes chewed in the leaves
answer: Yellow leaves, because it cannot make chlorophyll

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — KS3
ask: Complete the word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + ?
why: That is photosynthesis. The oxygen comes from splitting the water, and it is released as a waste product — which is where nearly all the oxygen in the air came from.

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — KS3
ask: Where in a plant cell does photosynthesis happen?
why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light. Leaf cells near the top of a leaf have the most, because that is where the light arrives.
choices: In the chloroplasts|In the nucleus|In the mitochondria|In the cell wall

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — KS3
ask: What does a plant use the glucose it makes for?
why: Glucose is the starting material for almost everything: respired for energy, stored as starch, built into cellulose for walls, and combined with nitrate to make proteins.
choices: Respiration, and for building starch and cellulose|Only for storing in the roots|Only for making oxygen|Nothing — it is a waste product
answer: Respiration, and for building starch and cellulose

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — KS3
ask: Respiration releases energy from glucose. Which gas does aerobic respiration need?
why: Aerobic means with oxygen. Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water — the exact reverse of photosynthesis, which is why the two fit together so neatly.
choices: Oxygen|Carbon dioxide|Nitrogen|Hydrogen

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — KS3
ask: Why do plants respire as well as photosynthesise?
why: Plants respire day and night. In bright light photosynthesis is faster, so the net effect is oxygen out; in the dark only respiration is happening, so it is carbon dioxide out.
choices: Every living cell needs energy all the time, including at night|They only respire when there is no light|Respiration makes their food|It is how they take in water
answer: Every living cell needs energy all the time, including at night

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which is the correct symbol equation for photosynthesis?
why: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆, so you need six carbons in and six waters to supply the twelve hydrogens. The second option is aerobic respiration — the same equation written backwards.
choices: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂|C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O|CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂|6CO₂ + 6O₂ → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Foundation
ask: Name one limiting factor of photosynthesis.
why: A limiting factor is whichever one is in shortest supply — raise it and the rate goes up, raise any other and nothing happens. That is why a greenhouse adds CO₂ and heat as well as light.
accept: light|light intensity|amount of light|temperature|carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide concentration|co2|co2 concentration|chlorophyll|amount of chlorophyll

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the product of anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
why: Without enough oxygen the glucose is only partly broken down, so much less energy is released and lactic acid builds up. Yeast does it differently — ethanol and carbon dioxide, which is fermentation.
choices: Lactic acid|Ethanol and carbon dioxide|Carbon dioxide and water|Glucose

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy than aerobic respiration?
why: Aerobic respiration takes glucose all the way to carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic stops at lactic acid, which still holds most of the energy — that is why it is a short-term option only.
choices: The glucose is not completely broken down|It happens at a lower temperature|It uses less glucose|It happens outside the cell
answer: The glucose is not completely broken down

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which piece of apparatus would you use to measure the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed?
why: Rate means amount per unit time, so you need something that counts a product — oxygen bubbles, or the volume of gas collected. Temperature and pH are variables to control, not the measurement.
choices: A gas syringe or measuring cylinder collecting the oxygen given off|A thermometer in the water|A pH meter|A balance measuring the mass of the pondweed
answer: A gas syringe or measuring cylinder collecting the oxygen given off

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Higher
ask: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a plant. By the inverse square law, the light intensity becomes...
why: Intensity ∝ 1/d². Doubling the distance spreads the same light over four times the area, so it is a quarter as intense — not half, which is the answer most people give first.
choices: a quarter of what it was|half of what it was|twice what it was|four times what it was
answer: a quarter of what it was

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Higher
ask: What is oxygen debt?
why: It is why you keep breathing hard after you stop. The blood carries the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose — and that oxidation is the debt being repaid.
choices: The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid|The oxygen used up during exercise|The oxygen a muscle stores before exercise|The carbon dioxide breathed out after exercise
answer: The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down lactic acid

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Higher
ask: What is metabolism?
why: It covers both directions — building starch, cellulose, lipids and proteins up, and breaking glucose and excess protein down. All of it is driven by energy from respiration.
choices: The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body|The breakdown of glucose only|The rate at which the heart beats|The building of protein from amino acids
answer: The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Higher
ask: Excess protein in the body is broken down. What is formed and where does it go?
why: Amino acids cannot be stored, so the amino group is removed — deamination — giving ammonia, which is toxic and is immediately converted to the much safer urea.
choices: Urea, formed in the liver and excreted by the kidneys|Ammonia, stored in the liver|Glucose, excreted in sweat|Lactic acid, broken down in the muscles
answer: Urea, formed in the liver and excreted by the kidneys

subject: Biology
name: Bioenergetics — GCSE Higher
ask: On a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity, the line levels off. What does that show?
why: A plateau means adding more of that factor changes nothing, so something else — temperature or carbon dioxide — has become the one in shortest supply.
choices: Light is no longer the limiting factor|The plant has stopped respiring|Light intensity has stopped increasing|The plant has run out of chlorophyll
answer: Light is no longer the limiting factor

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — KS3
ask: What is a reflex action?
why: The signal takes a short cut through the spinal cord instead of going to the conscious brain, which is why it is fast — and being fast is exactly the point when the stimulus is a hot pan.
choices: An automatic response that does not involve conscious thought|A response you have to decide to make|A slow response controlled by hormones|A response that only happens while asleep
answer: An automatic response that does not involve conscious thought

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — KS3
ask: Which organ detects light?
why: A sense organ contains receptor cells for one kind of stimulus. Light receptors are in the retina at the back of the eye.
choices: The eye|The ear|The skin|The tongue

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — KS3
ask: Why do you shiver when you are cold?
why: Shivering is muscles contracting and relaxing rapidly. Respiration is not fully efficient, so the extra respiration needed to power them releases heat — which is the point.
choices: Muscles contracting releases heat from respiration|It moves warm blood to the skin|It cools the body down faster|It stops sweat being produced
answer: Muscles contracting releases heat from respiration

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — KS3
ask: What is the name for keeping conditions inside the body steady?
why: Temperature, water, blood glucose — all held near a set point, because enzymes only work properly within a narrow range.

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — KS3
ask: Which system uses chemical messengers carried in the blood?
why: Hormones travel in the blood, so they are slower than nerves but last longer and reach the whole body. Nerve impulses are fast, brief and precisely targeted — the two systems suit different jobs.
choices: The endocrine system|The nervous system|The digestive system|The skeletal system

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Put the reflex arc in order: stimulus, response, receptor, effector, relay neurone, sensory neurone, motor neurone.
why: Sensory carries IN, motor carries OUT, relay joins them in the CNS. The effector is a muscle or a gland — whatever actually does the response.
choices: Stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response|Stimulus, receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector, response|Receptor, stimulus, sensory neurone, motor neurone, relay neurone, effector, response|Stimulus, sensory neurone, receptor, relay neurone, effector, motor neurone, response
answer: Stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector, response

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which hormone lowers blood glucose concentration?
why: Insulin is released by the pancreas when glucose is too high, and makes liver and muscle cells take glucose in and store it as glycogen. Glucagon does the opposite.

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Type 1 diabetes is caused by...
why: Type 1 is a supply problem, so it is treated with insulin injections. Type 2 is a response problem — the insulin is there and the cells ignore it — so it is managed with diet and exercise.
choices: the pancreas not producing enough insulin|the body cells not responding to insulin|eating too much sugar|the liver storing too much glycogen
answer: the pancreas not producing enough insulin

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which gland is often called the "master gland"?
why: It sits in the brain and releases hormones that control other glands — so it acts on the body mostly by telling the thyroid, ovaries and testes what to do.
choices: The pituitary gland|The thyroid gland|The pancreas|The adrenal gland

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Foundation
ask: What happens to the blood vessels near the skin when you are too hot?
why: That is vasodilation. The vessels themselves do not move — the arterioles supplying the surface capillaries simply widen, so more blood passes close to the air.
choices: They widen, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost|They narrow, so less heat is lost|They move closer to the bone|They stop carrying blood
answer: They widen, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: What is negative feedback?
why: It is the shape of every homeostatic system here — thyroxine, insulin and glucagon, temperature, water. Too high triggers lowering, too low triggers raising, so the level oscillates gently around a set point rather than drifting.
choices: A change away from the set point triggers a response that reverses it|A change is made larger by the response|The body ignores small changes|Two hormones are released at the same time
answer: A change away from the set point triggers a response that reverses it

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: Which hormone controls the amount of water reabsorbed by the kidney?
why: ADH is released by the pituitary when the blood is too concentrated. It makes the kidney tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and the urine is smaller in volume and more concentrated.

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: In the kidney, what happens during selective reabsorption?
why: Filtration is indiscriminate — glucose, ions, water and urea all leave the blood. Reabsorption is where the choosing happens: glucose is far too valuable to lose, so all of it comes back, and urea is left to go.
choices: All the glucose and some water and ions are taken back into the blood|Urea is taken back into the blood|Protein is filtered out of the blood|Water is removed from the blood
answer: All the glucose and some water and ions are taken back into the blood

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: A person is frightened. Which hormone is released and what does it do?
why: It is the fight-or-flight response, from the adrenal glands. Everything it does points one way: more respiration in the muscles, right now.
choices: Adrenaline — it increases heart rate and delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles|Insulin — it lowers blood glucose so the body can rest|Thyroxine — it slows the metabolic rate|ADH — it makes the kidneys produce more urine
answer: Adrenaline — it increases heart rate and delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles

subject: Biology
name: Homeostasis & Response — GCSE Higher
ask: Auxin collects on the shaded side of a shoot. What does the shoot do and why?
why: More elongation on the shaded side makes that side longer, so the shoot curves the other way — towards the light. In a root auxin does the reverse, inhibiting elongation, which is why roots grow down.
choices: It bends towards the light, because auxin makes those cells elongate more|It bends away from the light, because auxin kills the shaded cells|It grows straight up, because auxin is spread evenly|It stops growing until the light is even
answer: It bends towards the light, because auxin makes those cells elongate more

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — KS3
ask: In the food chain grass → rabbit → fox, what is the rabbit?
why: The producer is the grass, which makes its own food. The first thing to eat it is the primary consumer; the fox is the secondary consumer.
choices: A primary consumer|A producer|A predator only|A decomposer

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — KS3
ask: What does the arrow in a food chain show?
why: The arrow points from the thing eaten to the thing eating it — energy flowing that way. Drawing it backwards is the commonest mistake in the whole topic.
choices: The direction energy is transferred|Which animal is bigger|Which animal hunts first|The order the animals appeared

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — KS3
ask: What is a habitat?
why: Habitat is the place; population is all of one species there; community is all the species together; ecosystem is the community plus the non-living conditions.
choices: The place where an organism lives|All the organisms living in one place|The food an organism eats|A group of the same species
answer: The place where an organism lives

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — KS3
ask: Name one thing plants compete with each other for.
why: Plants compete for light, space, water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals compete for food, water, territory and mates — different lists, because they need different things.

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — KS3
ask: What do decomposers do?
why: Bacteria and fungi recycle the elements locked up in dead bodies and waste. Without them nothing would be released back, and the nutrients would run out.
choices: Break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil|Eat live animals|Make food using sunlight|Stop plants growing too fast
answer: Break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is a quadrat used for?
why: Counting everything is impossible, so you count a known area and scale up. Placing the quadrats randomly is what makes that scaling honest — choosing where to put them biases the answer.
choices: Sampling the number of organisms in a known area|Measuring light intensity|Measuring the pH of soil|Catching small animals
answer: Sampling the number of organisms in a known area

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Five quadrats of 1 m² contain 3, 5, 4, 6 and 2 daisies. Estimate the number in a 200 m² field.
why: Mean per m² = (3+5+4+6+2) ÷ 5 = 4. Then 4 × 200 = 800. Find the mean first, then scale — scaling one quadrat would be a guess with arithmetic on it.

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Name one abiotic factor that affects a community.
why: Abiotic means non-living — temperature, light, moisture, pH, wind, gas levels. Biotic factors are the living ones: predators, food, disease, competition.
accept: temperature|light|light intensity|water|moisture|ph|soil ph|wind|wind intensity|carbon dioxide|oxygen|mineral content|soil|rainfall

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
why: Photosynthesis is the only one on that list that takes carbon dioxide in. The other three all release it — which is why the balance between them is the whole carbon cycle.
choices: Photosynthesis|Respiration|Combustion|Decay

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is biodiversity important?
why: With many species, no one of them is essential to everything else — so losing one does not collapse the web. Low biodiversity means every link matters, which is fragile.
choices: A greater variety of species makes an ecosystem more stable|It makes ecosystems easier to count|It reduces the number of decomposers needed|It stops competition between species
answer: A greater variety of species makes an ecosystem more stable

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Higher
ask: Roughly what percentage of biomass is transferred from one trophic level to the next?
why: Most is lost as faeces, urea, and as heat from respiration; some of the level below is never eaten at all. That 90% loss each step is why food chains are rarely more than four or five links long.
choices: About 10%|About 50%|About 90%|About 1%

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Higher
ask: A trophic level has 20 000 kJ of biomass. The one above has 1 800 kJ. What is the efficiency of transfer?
why: 1800 ÷ 20000 = 0.09, so 9%. Efficiency is always the level above divided by the level below — getting it the other way up gives an answer over 100%, which is the tell.

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Higher
ask: Which conditions make decay fastest?
why: Decomposers are living things respiring, so they want what any organism wants — warmth for enzyme activity, water, and oxygen. Freezing, drying and sealing food are the three ways of preserving it, and each removes one of those.
choices: Warm, moist and with plenty of oxygen|Cold, dry and with plenty of oxygen|Warm, dry and with no oxygen|Cold, moist and with no oxygen
answer: Warm, moist and with plenty of oxygen

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Higher
ask: What does eutrophication do to a body of water?
why: The chain matters: nutrients → algal bloom → light blocked → plants die → decomposers multiply → oxygen used up → fish suffocate. The fertiliser never poisons anything directly.
choices: Fertiliser causes algae to bloom, and their decay uses up the oxygen|It makes the water more acidic so fish cannot breathe|It removes all the nutrients so plants die|It raises the temperature until fish die
answer: Fertiliser causes algae to bloom, and their decay uses up the oxygen

subject: Biology
name: Ecology — GCSE Higher
ask: Why can a pyramid of numbers be misleading where a pyramid of biomass is not?
why: A single oak feeding thousands of caterpillars gives an upside-down bar at the bottom. Biomass counts mass rather than individuals, so the tree outweighs the caterpillars and the pyramid comes out the right way up.
choices: One large producer such as a tree supports many consumers, so it is not pyramid-shaped|Numbers are harder to count accurately|Biomass is always measured in kilograms|Pyramids of number ignore decomposers
answer: One large producer such as a tree supports many consumers, so it is not pyramid-shaped

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — KS3
ask: Where in a cell is DNA found?
why: A chromosome is one long DNA molecule coiled up. A human body cell has 23 pairs — one of each pair from each parent.
choices: In the chromosomes inside the nucleus|In the cytoplasm only|In the cell membrane|In the mitochondria only
answer: In the chromosomes inside the nucleus

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — KS3
ask: What is a gene?
why: Gene → protein → characteristic. That chain is why a change in one gene can change something visible about a whole organism.
choices: A short section of DNA that codes for a protein|A whole chromosome|A type of cell|The male and female sex cells
answer: A short section of DNA that codes for a protein

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — KS3
ask: Which of these is an inherited characteristic?
why: Inherited characteristics are coded by genes passed from parents. The other three are acquired during life, so they are not passed on.
choices: Natural eye colour|A scar|A tattoo|Speaking French

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — KS3
ask: What are the sex cells in humans called?
why: The gametes are the sperm and the egg. Each carries half the usual number of chromosomes, so when they join the full number is restored.
accept: gametes|gamete|sperm and egg|egg and sperm|sperm and ova|sperm and ovum|sex cells

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — KS3
ask: Charles Darwin’s theory is called...
why: Individuals vary; those best suited survive and breed; their offspring inherit those features. Lamarck’s idea — that a characteristic gained in life is passed on — is the one that turned out to be wrong.
choices: natural selection|inheritance of acquired characteristics|spontaneous generation|selective breeding

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Foundation
ask: An allele that is expressed even when only one copy is present is called...
why: A recessive allele only shows when both copies are recessive. So a dominant characteristic can be carried by someone heterozygous, and a recessive one cannot be.
choices: dominant|recessive|homozygous|heterozygous

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Foundation
ask: A person has the genotype Bb. Are they homozygous or heterozygous?
why: Two different alleles is heterozygous; two the same — BB or bb — is homozygous.

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Foundation
ask: Two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) have a child. What fraction of offspring would be expected to show the recessive characteristic?
why: The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Only bb shows the recessive characteristic, so 1 in 4 — and 3 in 4 show the dominant one.
choices: 1 in 4|1 in 2|3 in 4|None

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Foundation
ask: How many chromosomes are in a human body cell?
why: 23 pairs, so 46 in total. A gamete has 23 — the single set — which is why a sperm and an egg together make 46 again.

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is selective breeding?
why: It is natural selection with a person doing the selecting. Repeated over generations it narrows the gene pool, which is why selectively bred animals are prone to inherited disease. Moving a gene is genetic engineering, and copying is cloning.
choices: Humans choosing which organisms breed, to get a desired characteristic|Organisms choosing their own mates|Moving a gene from one organism to another|Making identical copies of an organism
answer: Humans choosing which organisms breed, to get a desired characteristic

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Higher
ask: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele. Two carriers have a child. What is the probability the child has the disorder?
why: A carrier is heterozygous, so Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has the disorder — 25% — while 50% are carriers like their parents and 25% carry nothing.

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Higher
ask: How does meiosis differ from mitosis?
why: Two divisions, one copying — that is what halves the number. The differences come from the pairs separating at random and from crossing over, which is where the variation in sexual reproduction comes from.
choices: It makes four genetically different cells with half the chromosome number|It makes two identical cells with half the chromosome number|It makes four identical cells with the full chromosome number|It makes two different cells with the full chromosome number
answer: It makes four genetically different cells with half the chromosome number

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Higher
ask: What is speciation?
why: Isolation stops the gene pools mixing; different conditions select for different features; the differences accumulate. The test is fertile offspring — once that fails, they are two species.
choices: Two populations become so different they can no longer interbreed successfully|One species becoming extinct|A species moving to a new habitat|A gene being transferred between two species
answer: Two populations become so different they can no longer interbreed successfully

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Higher
ask: Why is a bacterium that survives an antibiotic a problem?
why: This is natural selection running in days rather than millennia, because bacteria divide so fast. The antibiotic does not cause the mutation — it selects the mutants that were already there.
choices: It reproduces rapidly and passes the resistance on, so a resistant strain spreads|It becomes larger than other bacteria|It makes the antibiotic poisonous|It can no longer be killed by the immune system
answer: It reproduces rapidly and passes the resistance on, so a resistant strain spreads

subject: Biology
name: Inheritance & Evolution — GCSE Higher
ask: In genetic engineering, what is used to cut a gene out of a chromosome?
why: Restriction enzymes cut the DNA, leaving sticky ends; ligase joins the gene into a vector — a plasmid or a virus — which carries it into the target cell. Enzymes do both the cutting and the joining.
choices: Enzymes|Acid|Heat|Electricity

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — KS3
ask: Which particle in an atom has a negative charge?
why: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge, electrons are negative. An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so overall it is neutral.
choices: Electron|Proton|Neutron|Nucleus

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — KS3
ask: Where in the atom is nearly all the mass?
why: Protons and neutrons each have a mass of 1; an electron is about 1/1836 of that. The nucleus is tiny compared with the atom and holds essentially all of it.
choices: In the nucleus|In the electrons|Spread evenly through the atom|In the outer shell

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — KS3
ask: What is an element?
why: A compound is elements chemically bonded — hard to separate. A mixture is just things together — easy to separate. An element is neither: one kind of atom, and nothing chemical will break it down.
choices: A substance made of only one type of atom|Two or more substances mixed together|Two or more elements chemically joined|Anything that can be separated by filtering
answer: A substance made of only one type of atom

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — KS3
ask: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of what?
why: The group number IS the number of outer electrons for the main groups — and because reactions are about outer electrons, that is why a group behaves alike.
accept: outer electrons|electrons in the outer shell|outer shell electrons|electrons in their outer shell|outer electron|valence electrons|outer shell

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — KS3
ask: Which of these is a metal?
why: Metals are on the left and middle of the periodic table. They conduct electricity and heat, are malleable, and form positive ions by losing electrons.
choices: Iron|Oxygen|Sulfur|Chlorine

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Foundation
ask: An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?
why: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12. The atomic number is the protons, and the mass number counts protons and neutrons together.

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Foundation
ask: What are isotopes?
why: Change the protons and you have changed the element. Neutrons change the mass and nothing else, so isotopes react identically — the chemistry is all in the electrons.
choices: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons|Atoms of the same element with different numbers of protons|Atoms of different elements with the same mass|Atoms that have lost an electron
answer: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why are Group 0 elements unreactive?
why: A full outer shell is a stable arrangement, so there is nothing to gain by reacting. Every other group reacts in order to reach that same arrangement.
choices: They have a full outer shell of electrons|They have only one outer electron|They are all gases|Their atoms are too heavy to react
answer: They have a full outer shell of electrons

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Foundation
ask: Going DOWN Group 1, the elements become...
why: A Group 1 atom reacts by LOSING its outer electron. Further down, that electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so it is more easily lost. Group 7 is the other way round, for the mirror-image reason.
choices: more reactive|less reactive|less metallic|harder to cut

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Foundation
ask: Write the electronic structure of an atom with 11 electrons.
why: Shells fill 2 then 8 then 8. Two outer electrons left over after 2 and 8 would be wrong — 11 − 10 = 1, so the outer shell holds one, which is why sodium is in Group 1.

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Higher
ask: Chlorine has isotopes of mass 35 (75%) and 37 (25%). What is its relative atomic mass?
why: A weighted mean: (35×75 + 37×25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5. A plain average of 35 and 37 would give 36 — the abundances are the whole point.

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Higher
ask: What did Rutherford’s alpha scattering experiment show?
why: Most alpha particles went straight through, so the atom is mostly empty; a few bounced back, so something small, heavy and positive is in there. That killed the plum pudding model. Bohr then added the fixed shells.
choices: The mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus|Electrons are spread through a ball of positive charge|Atoms are indivisible|Electrons orbit at fixed distances
answer: The mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Higher
ask: Why are transition metals often used as catalysts?
why: Being able to change charge and change back is what lets a catalyst take part in a reaction and be returned unchanged at the end.
choices: They can exist in more than one oxidation state|They have very low melting points|They are all magnetic|They react quickly with water
answer: They can exist in more than one oxidation state

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Higher
ask: Chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution. What happens?
why: Chlorine is higher in Group 7, so it is more reactive and takes the electron. Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂, and the bromine released is orange-brown.
choices: The chlorine displaces the bromine, and the solution turns orange|Nothing happens|The bromine displaces the chlorine|A white precipitate forms
answer: The chlorine displaces the bromine, and the solution turns orange

subject: Chemistry
name: Atomic Structure & the Periodic Table — GCSE Higher
ask: Why was Mendeleev’s periodic table accepted even though some elements were in the wrong order by atomic weight?
why: A prediction that later comes true is far stronger evidence than a tidy arrangement. The out-of-order pairs were explained later, when the table turned out to be ordered by proton number rather than weight.
choices: He left gaps and correctly predicted the properties of undiscovered elements|He listed more elements than anyone else|He arranged them alphabetically|He knew about protons
answer: He left gaps and correctly predicted the properties of undiscovered elements

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — KS3
ask: What holds the atoms together in a compound?
why: Bonds form when atoms transfer or share electrons to get a stable outer shell. Breaking them needs energy, which is why compounds are hard to split up.
choices: Chemical bonds|Gravity|Static electricity only|Magnetism

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — KS3
ask: Sodium chloride is made of sodium and chlorine. What type of substance is it?
why: The atoms are chemically joined, so the properties are nothing like the elements: sodium is a reactive metal, chlorine a poisonous gas, and together they are table salt.
choices: A compound|A mixture|An element|An isotope

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — KS3
ask: What does the formula H₂O tell you?
why: The small number applies to the symbol before it, and no number means one. So H₂O is two hydrogens and one oxygen.
choices: Two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom|Two hydrogen and two oxygen atoms|One hydrogen and two oxygen atoms|Hydrogen and oxygen mixed together
answer: Two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — KS3
ask: Why can metals be bent and hammered into shape?
why: The bonding is not directional — a sea of shared electrons holds the whole lattice — so sliding a layer does not break anything. In an ionic lattice sliding puts like charges together, which is why salt shatters instead.
choices: The layers of atoms can slide over each other|The atoms are very far apart|The bonds between atoms are weak|They are made of molecules
answer: The layers of atoms can slide over each other

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — KS3
ask: Which state of matter has particles that are close together but able to move past one another?
why: Solid: close and fixed in place. Liquid: close but free to move, which is why it flows and takes the shape of its container. Gas: far apart and moving fast in all directions.
choices: Liquid|Solid|Gas|None of them

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: What happens to electrons when an ionic bond forms?
why: The metal loses electrons to become a positive ion and the non-metal gains them to become negative. The bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between those opposite charges, in every direction — which is why it makes a giant lattice.
choices: They are transferred from the metal to the non-metal|They are shared between the two atoms|They are transferred from the non-metal to the metal|They are released into the air
answer: They are transferred from the metal to the non-metal

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why does sodium chloride conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?
why: Conducting needs charged particles that can MOVE. In a solid the ions are locked in the lattice; melting or dissolving frees them.
choices: The ions are free to move when molten|It gains electrons when it melts|It becomes a metal when molten|Heat carries the current
answer: The ions are free to move when molten

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: What type of bond holds the atoms together in a molecule of chlorine, Cl₂?
why: Two non-metals share a pair of electrons. Neither has anything to give to the other, so sharing is the only way both reach a full outer shell.
accept: covalent|covalent bond|a covalent bond|single covalent bond

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why does simple molecular carbon dioxide have a low boiling point?
why: Boiling separates molecules from one another — it does not break the covalent bonds inside them. The intermolecular forces are weak, so very little energy is needed.
choices: The forces between the molecules are weak|The covalent bonds inside the molecules are weak|It has no bonds at all|Its molecules are very heavy
answer: The forces between the molecules are weak

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon. Why is graphite soft?
why: Each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, leaving one electron free — which is why graphite also conducts. Diamond bonds all four, in a rigid 3-D network, so it is hard and does not conduct.
choices: Its layers have no bonds between them and can slide|Its carbon atoms have weaker covalent bonds|It contains no covalent bonds|Its atoms are further apart
answer: Its layers have no bonds between them and can slide

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the charge on an aluminium ion?
why: Aluminium is in Group 3, so it loses three electrons to empty its outer shell. Losing negatives leaves a 3+ charge.

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: Why can graphene and fullerenes be useful in nanotechnology?
why: A huge surface for very little material makes them good catalysts and good at carrying other molecules — drug delivery. It is also the property that makes their health effects uncertain.
choices: They have a very high surface area to volume ratio|They are extremely heavy|They melt at low temperatures|They are ionic
answer: They have a very high surface area to volume ratio

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: How does a polymer differ from a simple molecular substance in its melting point?
why: Intermolecular forces are weak per unit but there is far more of each molecule to attract, so the total is large. Polymers are still molecular, so they melt far below a giant covalent structure.
choices: Polymers melt higher, because the molecules are much larger|Polymers melt lower, because they are less dense|They melt at the same temperature|Polymers do not melt at all
answer: Polymers melt higher, because the molecules are much larger

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: Give the formula of magnesium oxide, given Mg forms Mg²⁺ and O forms O²⁻.
why: The charges are 2+ and 2−, so one of each cancels out. A compound must be neutral overall, which is the rule that sets every ionic formula.

subject: Chemistry
name: Bonding & Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: Why is a metal a good conductor of electricity?
why: The outer electrons leave their atoms and belong to the whole lattice. They can drift, which carries a current, and they can also carry energy, which is why metals conduct heat as well.
choices: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure|The positive ions move through the metal|The atoms vibrate and pass the current on|The metal is a giant covalent structure
answer: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — KS3
ask: In a sealed flask, 10 g of a chemical reacts with 15 g of another. What is the total mass at the end?
why: Mass is conserved: no atoms are created or destroyed, only rearranged. Sealing the flask is what makes it obvious — in an open one an escaping gas would look like lost mass.
choices: 25 g|15 g|10 g|It cannot be known

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — KS3
ask: What is the relative formula mass of water, H₂O? (H = 1, O = 16)
why: (2×1) + 16 = 18. Add every atom in the formula, counting each one as many times as the formula says.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — KS3
ask: Why does the mass seem to go DOWN when magnesium burns in an open crucible and some smoke escapes?
why: Nothing is destroyed — it has left the container. Weigh everything, including the gases, and the totals match. The same explanation, in reverse, is why magnesium usually gains mass: it has taken in oxygen from the air.
choices: Some of the product has escaped as a gas or smoke|Mass is destroyed when things burn|The magnesium evaporates|Oxygen has negative mass
answer: Some of the product has escaped as a gas or smoke

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — KS3
ask: How many atoms are in one molecule of CO₂?
why: One carbon and two oxygens. The small 2 applies only to the O immediately before it.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — KS3
ask: What does it mean to say an equation is balanced?
why: Balancing is conservation of mass written down. You may change the big numbers in front of a formula but never the small ones inside it, because that would change the substance.
choices: There are the same number of each type of atom on both sides|Both sides have the same number of molecules|The reaction goes both ways|The masses are written in grams
answer: There are the same number of each type of atom on both sides

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the relative formula mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
why: 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100. The commonest slip is forgetting that the 3 multiplies only the oxygen.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: How many moles are in 36 g of water? (Mᵣ of H₂O = 18)
why: Moles = mass ÷ Mᵣ = 36 ÷ 18 = 2. If the answer comes out enormous you have multiplied instead of divided.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the mass of 0.5 moles of sodium chloride? (Mᵣ of NaCl = 58.5)
why: Mass = moles × Mᵣ = 0.5 × 58.5 = 29.25 g. Half a mole is half the mass of one mole, which is a useful check.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the concentration, in g/dm³, of 20 g of solute in 0.5 dm³ of solution?
why: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40. Halving the volume doubles the concentration, so an answer smaller than 20 is the wrong way up.
choices: 40 g/dm³|10 g/dm³|20 g/dm³|0.025 g/dm³

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
why: A dm³ is a cube 10 cm on each side, so 10×10×10 = 1000 cm³. It is also exactly one litre.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 20 g but gives 15 g. What is the percentage yield?
why: 15 ÷ 20 × 100 = 75%. Actual over theoretical, always — the other way up gives over 100%, which cannot happen.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: Name one reason a reaction does not give a 100% yield.
why: Three real reasons: the reaction is reversible, some product is lost on handling, or there are side reactions giving something else. None of them is mass disappearing.
choices: The reaction is reversible, so it does not go to completion|Mass is destroyed during the reaction|The balanced equation is wrong|The reactants weigh more than the products
answer: The reaction is reversible, so it does not go to completion

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, how many moles of MgO are made from 0.4 moles of Mg?
why: The ratio of Mg to MgO in the equation is 2 : 2, which is 1 : 1 — so the moles of MgO equal the moles of Mg. Only the oxygen is in a different ratio.

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: What does "limiting reactant" mean?
why: The one that runs out sets the amount of product, however much of the other you have. That is why the yield is always calculated from the limiting reactant and never from the one in excess.
choices: The reactant that is completely used up, so it stops the reaction|The reactant present in the largest amount|The reactant with the highest relative formula mass|The reactant that is left over at the end
answer: The reactant that is completely used up, so it stops the reaction

subject: Chemistry
name: Quantitative Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: What is atom economy a measure of?
why: Atom economy is about the EQUATION — how much of what you put in is, on paper, the thing you want. Percentage yield is about the reaction as it actually ran. A reaction can have a perfect yield and a terrible atom economy.
choices: The proportion of the reactant mass that ends up as the useful product|How fast a reaction goes|How much product you actually get compared with the theoretical maximum|The cost of the reactants
answer: The proportion of the reactant mass that ends up as the useful product

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — KS3
ask: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strong acid?
why: Red is strongly acidic, green is neutral at pH 7, and blue to purple is alkaline. The scale runs 0 to 14.
choices: Red|Blue|Green|Purple

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — KS3
ask: Acid + alkali → salt + ?
why: That is neutralisation. The H⁺ from the acid and the OH⁻ from the alkali join to make water, which is why the pH moves towards 7.

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — KS3
ask: Which gas is given off when a metal reacts with an acid?
why: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The test is a lit splint, which gives a squeaky pop. A carbonate plus an acid gives carbon dioxide instead, which puts a splint out.
choices: Hydrogen|Oxygen|Carbon dioxide|Nitrogen

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — KS3
ask: Which of these is a sign that a chemical reaction has happened?
why: Melting, dissolving and changing shape are physical changes — reversible, no new substance. A chemical change makes something different, usually with a temperature change, a gas, a colour change or a precipitate as the clue.
choices: A new substance is formed that cannot easily be changed back|The substance changes shape|The substance is warmed up|The substance dissolves
answer: A new substance is formed that cannot easily be changed back

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — KS3
ask: Which metal is MORE reactive than the others?
why: The reactivity series runs potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold. Copper, silver and gold are so unreactive that gold is found as the metal itself.
choices: Magnesium|Copper|Silver|Gold

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is oxidation in terms of electrons?
why: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. Gaining oxygen is also oxidation, but the electron definition is the one that covers every case.
choices: Loss of electrons|Gain of electrons|Loss of protons|Gain of oxygen only

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive one from its compound. What happens if iron is put into copper sulfate solution?
why: Iron is above copper, so it takes the sulfate and pushes the copper out as metal. The blue colour is the copper ions in solution, so it fades as they leave.
choices: Copper is displaced and the blue solution fades|Nothing happens|Iron is displaced|The solution turns bright blue
answer: Copper is displaced and the blue solution fades

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: Name the salt made from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
why: The metal comes from the alkali and the rest of the name from the acid: hydrochloric gives chlorides, sulfuric gives sulfates, nitric gives nitrates.

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is produced at the negative electrode during electrolysis of a molten ionic compound?
why: Positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode — and metals form positive ions. Opposites attract is the whole rule.
choices: The metal|The non-metal|Water|Oxygen always

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by heating with carbon?
why: Carbon can only displace a metal below it in the reactivity series. Iron is below carbon, so a blast furnace works; aluminium is above, so it will not let go of its oxygen and electrolysis is the only route.
choices: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon|Aluminium oxide does not melt|Carbon is too expensive|Aluminium is found as the pure metal
answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: Write the half equation for what happens to a chloride ion at the positive electrode.
why: At the positive electrode negative ions LOSE electrons — oxidation — so the electrons go on the right. Two ions are needed to make one Cl₂ molecule.
choices: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻|Cl⁻ + e⁻ → Cl|Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻|2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: In the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution with inert electrodes, what is given off at the positive electrode?
why: With no halide present, the OH⁻ from the water is discharged instead, giving oxygen. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so at the negative electrode it is the copper that is deposited rather than hydrogen.
choices: Oxygen|Hydrogen|Copper|Sulfur

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
why: A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both perfectly possible. Strength is about what proportion of the molecules split into ions; concentration is about how many there are.
choices: Strong means fully ionised; concentrated means a lot of acid per dm³|They mean the same thing|Strong means a lot of acid per dm³; concentrated means fully ionised|Strong acids have a higher pH
answer: Strong means fully ionised; concentrated means a lot of acid per dm³

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: The pH of a solution falls from 5 to 2. The hydrogen ion concentration has...
why: The pH scale is logarithmic — each whole unit is a factor of ten. Three units down is 10³, so a thousandfold rise in H⁺.
choices: increased 1000 times|increased 3 times|decreased 1000 times|decreased 3 times

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: In a titration, why is the conical flask swirled during the addition?
why: Unmixed, a patch of unreacted acid can sit at the bottom and the indicator changes late — so the titre reads high. Adding dropwise near the end point is the other half of the same care.
choices: To mix the solutions so the end point is not missed|To keep the solution cool|To stop the burette leaking|To add oxygen to the reaction
answer: To mix the solutions so the end point is not missed

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — KS3
ask: A reaction makes the test tube feel hot. What kind of reaction is it?
why: Exo means out — energy leaves the reaction and warms the surroundings, which is what your hand feels. Endothermic takes energy in, so it feels cold.
choices: Exothermic|Endothermic|Reversible|Neutral

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — KS3
ask: Which of these is an exothermic process?
why: Combustion releases energy — that is the point of a fuel. Melting, photosynthesis and thermal decomposition all need energy putting in.
choices: Burning fuel|Melting ice|Photosynthesis|Thermal decomposition

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — KS3
ask: Name one everyday use of an exothermic reaction.
why: Hand warmers and self-heating cans use an exothermic reaction deliberately. Sports injury packs use the opposite — an endothermic one that draws heat out.
accept: hand warmer|hand warmers|handwarmer|self heating can|self-heating can|burning fuel|combustion|fuel|heating|burning|a fire|fire|central heating

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — KS3
ask: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction?
why: The reaction takes energy IN from the surroundings, so the surroundings lose it. That is why an endothermic mixture feels cold.
choices: It falls|It rises|It stays the same|It rises then falls

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — KS3
ask: Why does a fire need energy to start even though burning gives out energy?
why: Breaking bonds always takes energy in; making them always gives energy out. A fire has to be started because the breaking comes first — after that, the energy released keeps it going.
choices: Energy is needed first to break the bonds in the fuel|Fires only release energy after ten minutes|The match adds fuel|Oxygen has to be heated to react
answer: Energy is needed first to break the bonds in the fuel

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, where are the products?
why: The drop IS the energy released. Endothermic profiles go up, because energy has been taken in and stored in the products.
choices: Lower than the reactants|Higher than the reactants|At the same level as the reactants|At the top of the curve

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is activation energy?
why: It is the hump on the profile. A collision with less than that just bounces — which is why raising the temperature speeds a reaction up, since more particles clear the hump.
choices: The minimum energy needed for particles to react when they collide|The energy released by a reaction|The energy stored in the products|The difference between reactants and products
answer: The minimum energy needed for particles to react when they collide

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: Breaking bonds is...
why: Breaking takes energy in; making gives energy out. Whether the whole reaction is exo or endo depends on which of the two is bigger.
choices: endothermic|exothermic|neither|always exothermic in fuels

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: A reaction releases more energy making bonds than it takes breaking them. The reaction is...
why: More out than in means the surplus leaves as heat. That is the bond-energy way of saying what the profile shows by going downhill.
choices: exothermic|endothermic|at equilibrium|impossible

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Foundation
ask: Name one use of an endothermic reaction.
why: A cold pack uses an endothermic process to take heat out of an injury. It is the exact mirror of a hand warmer.
accept: cold pack|sports injury pack|instant cold pack|ice pack|cooling pack|sports injury cold pack|chemical cold pack|cooling an injury

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: Bond energies: breaking takes 2500 kJ, making releases 2800 kJ. What is the overall energy change?
why: Energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 2500 − 2800 = −300 kJ. A negative answer means energy left the reaction, so it is exothermic — the sign is the answer to the second half of the question.
choices: −300 kJ, exothermic|+300 kJ, endothermic|−300 kJ, endothermic|+5300 kJ, exothermic

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: In a chemical cell, what determines the size of the voltage produced?
why: The further apart the two metals are in the reactivity series, the bigger the potential difference. Two of the same metal gives no voltage at all.
choices: The difference in reactivity between the two metals|The size of the electrodes|The colour of the electrolyte|The temperature of the room only
answer: The difference in reactivity between the two metals

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: What is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a rechargeable battery?
why: A fuel cell keeps going as long as hydrogen and oxygen arrive, and the only product is water. The real problems are storing hydrogen safely and making it without using fossil fuels.
choices: It does not run down or need recharging while fuel is supplied|It produces no water|Hydrogen is easy to store|It works without oxygen
answer: It does not run down or need recharging while fuel is supplied

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
why: Hydrogen is oxidised to water, and the energy released drives the current. It is combustion with the energy taken as electricity rather than as heat.
choices: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O|H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂|2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂|H₂ + O → H₂O

subject: Chemistry
name: Energy Changes — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction have a lower hump?
why: The reactants and products sit exactly where they did — the overall energy change is unchanged. Only the path between them is easier, so more collisions succeed.
choices: The catalyst provides a different route with a lower activation energy|The catalyst releases energy into the reaction|The catalyst lowers the energy of the products|The catalyst removes some of the reactants
answer: The catalyst provides a different route with a lower activation energy

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — KS3
ask: Which of these makes a reaction go faster?
why: Hotter particles move faster, so they collide more often and harder. The other three all slow a reaction down.
choices: Raising the temperature|Using larger lumps|Using a more dilute acid|Cooling the mixture

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — KS3
ask: Why does powdered chalk react faster with acid than a single lump?
why: A reaction can only happen where the two substances touch. Grinding a lump up exposes the inside, so far more particles are available to collide at once.
choices: The powder has a larger surface area|The powder is heavier|The powder is a different chemical|Powder dissolves the acid
answer: The powder has a larger surface area

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — KS3
ask: What is a catalyst?
why: Because it is not used up, a tiny amount works over and over — which is why catalysts are worth their cost in industry.
choices: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up|A substance that slows a reaction down|A substance that is used up in a reaction|A type of acid
answer: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — KS3
ask: How could you measure how fast a reaction that gives off a gas is going?
why: Rate is an amount per unit time, so you need a quantity you can measure repeatedly. Gas volume in a syringe, or mass lost on a balance, both work.
choices: Measure the volume of gas collected each minute|Measure the colour of the liquid|Measure the temperature of the room|Count the bubbles that burst
answer: Measure the volume of gas collected each minute

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — KS3
ask: Two reactions produce the same amount of gas. One finishes in 20 s and one in 60 s. Which is faster?
why: Same amount, less time, so more per second. A steeper line on a graph of gas against time means exactly this.
choices: The 20 s one|The 60 s one|They are the same speed|It cannot be known

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Foundation
ask: According to collision theory, a reaction happens when particles...
why: Both halves matter — they must meet AND meet hard enough. Every factor that speeds a reaction up works by changing the frequency of collisions, their energy, or both.
choices: collide with at least the activation energy|collide at any speed|are heated above 100 °C|are in the same state of matter
answer: collide with at least the activation energy

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Foundation
ask: 48 cm³ of gas is produced in 60 seconds. What is the mean rate?
why: 48 ÷ 60 = 0.8. Rate is always amount ÷ time — dividing the other way gives seconds per cm³, which is a different quantity.
choices: 0.8 cm³/s|1.25 cm³/s|8 cm³/s|2880 cm³/s

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Foundation
ask: On a graph of gas volume against time, what does the line doing when the reaction has finished?
why: No more gas is being made, so the volume stops changing. The steepest part is at the start, where the reactants are most concentrated.
choices: It becomes horizontal|It becomes steeper|It goes downwards|It stops being drawn

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Foundation
ask: Increasing the concentration of a solution speeds up a reaction because...
why: Concentration changes how CROWDED it is, not how fast the particles move. Temperature is the one that changes speed — and it raises both frequency and energy, which is why it has such a large effect.
choices: there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent|the particles move faster|the activation energy is lowered|the particles are bigger
