answer: there are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Foundation
ask: In the reaction of sodium thiosulfate with acid, what is observed?
why: Timing how long a cross beneath the flask takes to disappear is the classic rate experiment — the cloudiness is a precipitate of sulfur, so the time is a measure of the rate.
choices: The solution turns cloudy as sulfur is formed|A gas is given off and the mixture fizzes|The solution turns bright blue|A metal is deposited
answer: The solution turns cloudy as sulfur is formed

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Higher
ask: How do you find the rate at a particular moment from a curved rate graph?
why: The mean rate is the overall gradient; the rate AT a moment is the gradient of the curve there, which is what a tangent measures. On a curve those two are different numbers.
choices: Draw a tangent at that point and find its gradient|Divide the final volume by the final time|Measure the height of the curve at that point|Find the area under the curve
answer: Draw a tangent at that point and find its gradient

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Higher
ask: What does Le Chatelier’s principle say happens if the pressure is increased on a gaseous equilibrium?
why: The system opposes the change, and making fewer gas molecules lowers the pressure again. If both sides have equal numbers of gas molecules, pressure changes nothing.
choices: The position shifts towards the side with fewer molecules of gas|The position shifts towards the side with more molecules of gas|The equilibrium is unaffected by pressure|Both forward and backward reactions stop
answer: The position shifts towards the side with fewer molecules of gas

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Higher
ask: A forward reaction is exothermic. What happens to the yield if the temperature is raised?
why: The system opposes the rise by absorbing energy, which means going backwards. Note the trap: the reaction gets FASTER and the YIELD gets smaller — rate and yield are two different questions.
choices: It decreases, because the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction|It increases, because the reaction goes faster|It stays the same|It increases, because heat favours exothermic reactions
answer: It decreases, because the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Higher
ask: What does it mean to say a reaction is at dynamic equilibrium?
why: Dynamic means nothing has stopped — molecules are converting in both directions constantly, and the concentrations hold steady because the two rates match. It does not mean equal amounts.
choices: Both reactions are still happening, at the same rate|Both reactions have stopped|The amounts of reactant and product are equal|The forward reaction has finished
answer: Both reactions are still happening, at the same rate

subject: Chemistry
name: Rate of Reaction — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a catalyst not change the position of an equilibrium?
why: The lower-energy route works in both directions, so equilibrium arrives sooner and in exactly the same place. A catalyst buys time, not yield.
choices: It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally|It is used up before equilibrium is reached|It only works on the forward reaction|It changes the activation energy of only one direction
answer: It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — KS3
ask: What is a pure substance?
why: Chemistry uses pure in a stricter sense than a label on a bottle does. Pure orange juice is a mixture; pure water is one compound and nothing else.
choices: A single element or compound, not mixed with anything else|Anything that is safe to drink|A substance that dissolves in water|Anything found in nature
answer: A single element or compound, not mixed with anything else

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — KS3
ask: In chromatography, what happens to the substance that is MOST attracted to the paper?
why: A substance is pulled two ways — the solvent carries it up, the paper holds it back. The more the paper wins, the less far it goes.
choices: It travels the shortest distance|It travels the furthest|It stays dissolved in the solvent|It does not move at all

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — KS3
ask: Why is the starting line in chromatography drawn in pencil?
why: An ink line would run up the paper with the samples and separate into its own spots, which is exactly what the experiment is trying to measure elsewhere.
choices: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent|Pencil is easier to see|Pen is too thick|Pencil makes the paper absorb faster
answer: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — KS3
ask: A substance melts sharply at exactly 80 °C. What does that suggest?
why: A pure substance melts and boils at a fixed temperature. A mixture melts over a range and usually lower than the pure substance — which is why salt on a road stops ice forming.
choices: It is pure|It is a mixture|It is a metal|It contains water

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — KS3
ask: How would you test for carbon dioxide?
why: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution; CO₂ makes insoluble calcium carbonate, which is the cloudiness. The other three are the tests for hydrogen, chlorine and oxygen.
choices: Bubble it through limewater and see if it turns cloudy|Put a lit splint in it|Hold damp litmus paper in it|See if it relights a glowing splint
answer: Bubble it through limewater and see if it turns cloudy

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the test for oxygen?
why: A glowing splint has stopped flaming but is still hot; extra oxygen is enough to restart it. Hydrogen is the squeaky pop, CO₂ the limewater, chlorine the bleaching.
choices: It relights a glowing splint|It gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint|It turns limewater cloudy|It bleaches damp litmus paper

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Foundation
ask: A spot travels 4 cm and the solvent front travels 8 cm. What is the Rₑ value?
why: Rₑ = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5. It is always between 0 and 1, so an answer above 1 is the division the wrong way up.

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why can Rₑ values identify a substance?
why: The conditions are part of the measurement — change the solvent and the values all change, which is why a reference sample is run on the same paper.
choices: For a given solvent and paper, a substance always gives the same value|Every substance has an Rₑ of exactly 1|Rₑ depends only on the colour|Rₑ is the same in every solvent
answer: For a given solvent and paper, a substance always gives the same value

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Foundation
ask: What colour flame does sodium give in a flame test?
why: Lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green. Sodium is so bright it can mask the others, which is a real limitation of the test.
choices: Yellow|Lilac|Crimson|Green

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Foundation
ask: A chromatogram of ink shows four spots. Is the ink pure?
why: One spot means one substance. Four spots is four things travelling at four different rates — and it is at least four, because two substances can share an Rₑ value.
choices: No, it is a mixture of at least four substances|Yes, pure substances give several spots|It cannot be told from a chromatogram|Yes, provided the spots are the same colour
answer: No, it is a mixture of at least four substances

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Higher
ask: How do you test for a carbonate ion?
why: Carbonates fizz with acid, giving CO₂, which turns limewater cloudy. The other three are the tests for ammonium, halides and sulfates.
choices: Add dilute acid and test the gas with limewater|Add sodium hydroxide and warm it|Add silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid|Add barium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid
answer: Add dilute acid and test the gas with limewater

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Higher
ask: Silver nitrate solution is added to a halide. A cream precipitate forms. Which halide is it?
why: Chloride is white, bromide cream, iodide yellow — three shades that darken down the group. Dilute nitric acid is added first to remove carbonates, which would give their own precipitate.
choices: Bromide|Chloride|Iodide|Fluoride

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Higher
ask: A white precipitate forms with barium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid. Which ion is present?
why: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so it drops out as a white solid. The acid is there to remove any carbonate first, which would otherwise give a white precipitate too.
choices: Sulfate|Carbonate|Chloride|Nitrate

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Higher
ask: Give one advantage of instrumental methods such as flame emission spectroscopy.
why: They also identify several ions in one mixture, which a flame test cannot — sodium swamps everything. The cost is expensive equipment and trained operators.
choices: They are accurate, sensitive and rapid, and work on tiny samples|They need no electricity|They are cheaper than a flame test|They do not need a reference sample
answer: They are accurate, sensitive and rapid, and work on tiny samples

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemical Analysis — GCSE Higher
ask: Sodium hydroxide is added to a solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which metal ion is present?
why: Copper(II) blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) brown, and calcium, magnesium and aluminium all white — with aluminium alone redissolving in excess sodium hydroxide, which is how it is told from the other two.
choices: Copper(II)|Iron(II)|Iron(III)|Calcium

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — KS3
ask: Which method separates sand from water?
why: Sand is insoluble, so its particles are too big to pass through the filter paper while water molecules go straight through. Filtration only works on something undissolved.
choices: Filtration|Distillation|Chromatography|Evaporation

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — KS3
ask: How would you get salt back from salty water?
why: Dissolved salt passes through a filter with the water, so filtering does nothing. Evaporating drives the water off and leaves the salt behind as crystals.
choices: Evaporate the water|Filter it|Use a magnet|Add more water

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — KS3
ask: What is the residue in filtration?
why: Residue stays, filtrate passes through. Which one you want decides whether you keep the paper or the beaker.
choices: The solid left in the filter paper|The liquid that passes through|The dissolved substance|The filter paper itself
answer: The solid left in the filter paper

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — KS3
ask: Distillation separates two liquids using a difference in what?
why: The one with the lower boiling point turns to vapour first, travels to the condenser and is collected. Filtration and chromatography use different properties entirely.
accept: boiling point|boiling points|boiling temperature|their boiling points|bp

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — KS3
ask: What is a solvent?
why: Solute dissolves in solvent to make a solution. In salty water the salt is the solute and the water is the solvent.
choices: The liquid a substance dissolves in|The substance that dissolves|A mixture of a solid and a liquid|A solid that will not dissolve
answer: The liquid a substance dissolves in

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is crystallisation better than simple evaporation for getting pure crystals?
why: Evaporating to dryness traps impurities in the solid. Heating to saturation and then cooling slowly gives the crystals time to form in an orderly way, leaving impurities in the remaining liquid.
choices: Slow cooling lets larger, purer crystals form|It works faster|It needs no heat at all|It removes insoluble impurities
answer: Slow cooling lets larger, purer crystals form

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Foundation
ask: In fractional distillation of a liquid mixture, what comes off first?
why: It vaporises at the lowest temperature, so as the mixture is heated it leaves first. The fractionating column lets the higher-boiling vapours condense and fall back.
choices: The liquid with the lowest boiling point|The liquid with the highest boiling point|The densest liquid|The liquid present in the greatest amount
answer: The liquid with the lowest boiling point

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which separation method would you use for a mixture of coloured dyes?
why: The dyes are all dissolved, so filtration cannot touch them, and their boiling points are too close for distillation. Chromatography separates them on how strongly each is attracted to the paper.
choices: Chromatography|Filtration|Distillation|Crystallisation

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Foundation
ask: In distillation, what is the purpose of the condenser?
why: Cold water runs through the outer jacket — in at the bottom, out at the top, so the jacket stays full. Without it the vapour escapes and nothing is collected.
choices: To cool the vapour back into a liquid|To heat the mixture|To filter out solids|To measure the boiling point
answer: To cool the vapour back into a liquid

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Foundation
ask: How could you separate iron filings from sand?
why: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so one property separates them without any chemistry at all. Choosing the method means finding the property that differs.
accept: magnet|use a magnet|with a magnet|magnetism|a magnet

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Higher
ask: Why can fractional distillation separate liquids with very similar boiling points when simple distillation cannot?
why: Each cycle enriches the vapour a little in the more volatile component. A tall column is many small separations stacked, which is what makes a fine difference workable.
choices: The column gives repeated evaporation and condensation up its length|The column is heated more strongly|The column removes the solvent|The column filters the vapour
answer: The column gives repeated evaporation and condensation up its length

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Higher
ask: In the distillation of sea water, where should the thermometer bulb be placed?
why: You are measuring the temperature of the VAPOUR leaving, because that is what is being collected. In the liquid it reads the mixture, which is not the same thing.
choices: At the entrance to the condenser|In the liquid being heated|Inside the collecting flask|Touching the bottom of the flask
answer: At the entrance to the condenser

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Higher
ask: A solution is filtered, then the filtrate is crystallised. What has been separated?
why: Filtration only removes what is undissolved, so anything in solution passes through and has to be dealt with separately. Two steps, two different properties.
choices: An insoluble solid first, then the dissolved solid from the solvent|Two dissolved solids from each other|Two liquids from each other|A gas from a liquid
answer: An insoluble solid first, then the dissolved solid from the solvent

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Higher
ask: Why is paper chromatography described as having a stationary and a mobile phase?
why: Separation comes from how each substance divides between the two — held by the stationary phase or carried by the mobile one. That balance is what the Rₑ value measures.
choices: The paper stays still while the solvent moves through it|The spots stay still while the paper moves|The paper moves while the solvent stays still|Both phases move at the same speed
answer: The paper stays still while the solvent moves through it

subject: Chemistry
name: Separating Mixtures — GCSE Higher
ask: Potable water is not pure water. Why not?
why: Potable means safe to drink, which is a standard about harm. Pure means one substance only — and distilled water, which is pure, tastes flat and is not what anybody supplies.
choices: It still contains dissolved salts and other substances at safe levels|It contains bacteria|It has been distilled|It contains no oxygen
answer: It still contains dissolved salts and other substances at safe levels

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — KS3
ask: What is crude oil mainly made of?
why: A hydrocarbon contains hydrogen and carbon only. Crude oil is a mixture of thousands of them, formed from the remains of ancient plankton.
choices: Hydrocarbons|Metals|Salts|Carbohydrates

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — KS3
ask: Crude oil is a...
why: It takes millions of years to form, so it is being used far faster than it is made. Finite is the reason for both the price and the search for alternatives.
choices: finite resource|renewable resource|pure substance|metal ore

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — KS3
ask: Which gas is produced when a hydrocarbon burns completely?
why: Complete combustion oxidises every carbon to CO₂ and every hydrogen to H₂O. With too little oxygen you get carbon monoxide and soot instead.
choices: Carbon dioxide and water vapour|Carbon monoxide only|Hydrogen only|Nitrogen

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — KS3
ask: What is the name for the process that separates crude oil into fractions?
why: Different hydrocarbons have different boiling points, so they condense at different heights up the column — shorter chains near the cool top, longer ones at the hot bottom.

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — KS3
ask: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
why: It binds to haemoglobin better than oxygen does, so the blood stops carrying oxygen. Having no colour and no smell is what makes it a killer rather than a hazard.
choices: It is toxic and cannot be seen or smelled|It burns explosively|It turns the air acidic|It damages the ozone layer
answer: It is toxic and cannot be seen or smelled

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the general formula of an alkane?
why: Alkanes are saturated — single bonds only — so each carbon carries as many hydrogens as it can. CₙH₂ₙ is the alkene formula, which is two hydrogens short because of the double bond.
choices: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂|CₙH₂ₙ|CₙHₙ|CₙH₂ₙ₋₂

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: How many carbon atoms does propane have?
why: Meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4. The prefix names the chain length, and the ending says which family.

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the test for an alkene?
why: The bromine adds across the C=C double bond, so the colour disappears. An alkane has no double bond and leaves the bromine water orange.
choices: It turns bromine water from orange to colourless|It turns limewater cloudy|It gives a squeaky pop|It relights a glowing splint
answer: It turns bromine water from orange to colourless

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: Going UP the fractions from petrol to bitumen, the hydrocarbons become...
why: Longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces, so they boil higher, flow less easily and ignite less readily. Every one of those trends comes from the same cause.
choices: less volatile and more viscous|more volatile and less viscous|lighter in colour|easier to ignite

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is cracking?
why: Fractional distillation gives too much of the long fractions and not enough petrol. Cracking fixes the mismatch, and the alkenes it also produces are the raw material for polymers.
choices: Breaking long hydrocarbon chains into shorter, more useful ones|Joining short chains into long ones|Burning crude oil to release energy|Separating crude oil into fractions
answer: Breaking long hydrocarbon chains into shorter, more useful ones

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the functional group of an alcohol?
why: –OH makes an alcohol, –COOH a carboxylic acid, C=C an alkene. The functional group is what the family’s reactions come from, whatever the chain length.
choices: –OH|–COOH|C=C|–NH₂

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: What is produced when ethanol is oxidised?
why: It happens in air over time, which is why wine turns to vinegar. Ethanoic acid is what vinegar is.
choices: Ethanoic acid|Ethene|Ethane|Ethyl ethanoate

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: Addition polymerisation requires the monomer to have...
why: The double bond opens and the units join in a chain, with no other product at all. Condensation polymerisation is the other kind — two functional groups and a small molecule such as water released each time.
choices: a carbon-carbon double bond|two functional groups|an –OH group|at least six carbon atoms

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: Ethene reacts with steam to make which substance?
why: Hydration, with a catalyst, at high temperature and pressure. The alternative route is fermenting sugar with yeast — cheaper and renewable, but slower and giving a less pure product.
choices: Ethanol|Ethane|Ethanoic acid|Ethyl ethanoate

subject: Chemistry
name: Organic Chemistry — GCSE Higher
ask: Why are some polymers difficult to dispose of?
why: The very inertness that makes a polymer useful — it does not rot, rust or react — is what leaves it in landfill for centuries. That is the trade-off the whole disposal problem rests on.
choices: They are unreactive so they are not biodegradable|They dissolve in ground water|They give off toxic gas at room temperature|They react with soil minerals
answer: They are unreactive so they are not biodegradable

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — KS3
ask: Roughly what percentage of the air is nitrogen?
why: About 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour making up the rest. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%, which is why a small change in it matters so much proportionally.

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — KS3
ask: Which gas do we need for respiration?
why: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose. Nitrogen is the commonest gas in air and is almost completely unreactive.
choices: Oxygen|Nitrogen|Carbon dioxide|Argon

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — KS3
ask: Name one greenhouse gas.
why: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb the long-wavelength radiation the Earth gives off and re-emit some of it downwards, which keeps the surface warm.

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — KS3
ask: What is the main cause of the rise in carbon dioxide over the last 200 years?
why: Fossil fuels are carbon that was locked away for millions of years. Burning them returns it to the atmosphere far faster than photosynthesis and the oceans can take it out. Deforestation makes it worse by removing the things that would.
choices: Burning fossil fuels|Volcanic eruptions|Plants dying|Changes in the Sun

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — KS3
ask: Which gas causes acid rain?
why: Sulfur impurities in fuel burn to sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in cloud water to make an acid. Oxides of nitrogen, made by the heat of an engine, do the same.
choices: Sulfur dioxide|Carbon dioxide|Nitrogen|Oxygen

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Foundation
ask: Where is the oxygen in the Earth’s early atmosphere thought to have come from?
why: The early atmosphere was mostly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen. Algae appeared about 2.7 billion years ago and released oxygen as a waste product — the whole of the oxygen we breathe is biological in origin.
choices: Photosynthesis by early algae and plants|Volcanic activity|Water evaporating from the oceans|Meteorite impacts
answer: Photosynthesis by early algae and plants

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Foundation
ask: How did the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decrease over billions of years?
why: Sedimentary rocks like limestone are carbon that came out of the air, and so are coal, oil and gas. Burning fossil fuels is putting some of it straight back.
choices: It dissolved in the oceans and was locked into rocks and fossil fuels|It escaped into space|It reacted with nitrogen|It was broken down by sunlight
answer: It dissolved in the oceans and was locked into rocks and fossil fuels

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which of these is a consequence of global climate change?
why: Sea level rises two ways at once — ice that was on land adds water, and warmer water takes up more room. Changing rainfall patterns and shifting species are the other effects.
choices: Rising sea levels from melting ice and thermal expansion|A fall in the amount of nitrogen in the air|The Sun getting hotter|More argon in the atmosphere
answer: Rising sea levels from melting ice and thermal expansion

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is a carbon footprint?
why: Whole life means making, using, transporting and disposing of it — so a product that is clean to use can still have a large footprint. Measuring every stage accurately is what makes it hard to pin down.
choices: The total greenhouse gases released over the whole life of a product or service|The mass of carbon in a fuel|The carbon dioxide in a room|The amount of carbon in the soil
answer: The total greenhouse gases released over the whole life of a product or service

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is carbon monoxide produced by incomplete combustion?
why: Short of oxygen, some carbon reaches only CO and some none at all, which is the soot. That is why a blocked flue or a badly serviced boiler is dangerous.
choices: There is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon fully|The fuel is burned at too high a temperature|The fuel contains carbon monoxide already|Water vapour gets in the way
answer: There is not enough oxygen to oxidise all the carbon fully

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Higher
ask: Why are peer-reviewed climate models more reliable than a single opinion?
why: Peer review is the mechanism that catches a mistake before it is believed. Early models were genuinely incomplete, and that is why reporting in the media — often simplified or biased — is not the same as the evidence.
choices: Other scientists check the data and reasoning independently|They always give the same answer|They are produced by governments|They ignore uncertain data
answer: Other scientists check the data and reasoning independently

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Higher
ask: What does "carbon neutral" mean?
why: Burning a biofuel releases CO₂ the crop took in while growing, so in principle it balances. In practice the fuel used to farm and transport it has to be counted too.
choices: Any carbon dioxide released is balanced by an equal amount removed|No carbon dioxide is released at all|Only carbon monoxide is released|The carbon is stored as a solid
answer: Any carbon dioxide released is balanced by an equal amount removed

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Higher
ask: Give one way a country could reduce its carbon footprint.
why: Other real routes are carbon capture and storage, better efficiency, and carbon taxes. The obstacles are usually cost, the scientific work still needed, and whether people will change how they live.
choices: Use renewable energy sources instead of fossil fuels|Cut down more forest for farmland|Increase the use of coal-fired power|Export more manufactured goods
answer: Use renewable energy sources instead of fossil fuels

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Higher
ask: Why do oxides of nitrogen form inside a car engine?
why: Nitrogen is normally very unreactive; the heat of combustion is enough to overcome that. The nitrogen comes from the air drawn in, not from the fuel.
choices: The high temperature makes nitrogen and oxygen from the air react|Nitrogen is present in petrol|The catalytic converter produces them|They come from the oil in the engine
answer: The high temperature makes nitrogen and oxygen from the air react

subject: Chemistry
name: Chemistry of the Atmosphere — GCSE Higher
ask: Particulates released by burning fuels cause...
why: Solid particles reflect sunlight back into space, which is global dimming, and lodge in the lungs. Acid rain is sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides — a different pollutant with a different effect.
choices: global dimming and health problems such as lung damage|acid rain|the greenhouse effect|ozone depletion
answer: global dimming and health problems such as lung damage

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — KS3
ask: Which of these is a renewable resource?
why: Renewable means it is replaced at least as fast as it is used. Replanting is what makes wood renewable; fossil fuels take millions of years and are not.
choices: Wood from a managed forest|Coal|Crude oil|Natural gas

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — KS3
ask: Why is recycling metal better than extracting it from ore?
why: Extraction means mining, transporting and then reducing the ore — all of it expensive in energy. Melting scrap skips nearly all of that, and the ore is finite.
choices: It uses much less energy and conserves the ore|Recycled metal is stronger|It produces more metal overall|It requires no sorting
answer: It uses much less energy and conserves the ore

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — KS3
ask: Name one thing added to water to make it safe to drink.
why: Sterilising kills microbes, using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light. Filtering comes first to remove solids — one step for the visible, one for the invisible.

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — KS3
ask: What is potable water?
why: Potable is a standard about safety, not purity — drinking water still contains dissolved salts, and that is fine.
choices: Water that is safe to drink|Water with nothing dissolved in it|Water taken from the sea|Water that has been boiled
answer: Water that is safe to drink

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — KS3
ask: Why do we treat waste water before returning it to rivers?
why: Untreated sewage carries pathogens and feeds bacteria that then use up the river’s oxygen. Treatment screens the solids out, settles the sludge and digests it biologically.
choices: To remove harmful microbes and chemicals that would damage wildlife|To make it taste better|To make it colder|To add oxygen to the river
answer: To remove harmful microbes and chemicals that would damage wildlife

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Foundation
ask: How is potable water usually produced in the UK?
why: The UK has enough rain, so fresh water is cheap to treat. Desalination — distillation or reverse osmosis — is only used where there is no fresh source, because it needs a great deal of energy.
choices: Choose a fresh water source, filter it, then sterilise it|Distil sea water|Filter sea water only|Add salt then evaporate it
answer: Choose a fresh water source, filter it, then sterilise it

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is a life cycle assessment?
why: Raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal. Some of it is measurable — energy, water, waste — and some, such as the effect of a pollutant, is a judgement, which is why an LCA can be slanted to support a claim.
choices: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life|A test of how long a product lasts|A measure of how much a product costs|A check on whether a product can be recycled
answer: An assessment of the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Foundation
ask: Rusting needs which two substances?
why: Remove either and iron does not rust, which is why oil, grease, paint and plastic all work as protection: they keep both out.
choices: Water and oxygen|Water and carbon dioxide|Oxygen and nitrogen|Acid and oxygen

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why does galvanising protect iron even if the coating is scratched?
why: That is sacrificial protection. Paint only works while it is intact; zinc goes on protecting after the barrier has failed, because the protection is chemical rather than physical.
choices: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron|Zinc seals the scratch automatically|Zinc is harder than iron|Zinc repels water
answer: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is an alloy?
why: The different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so they cannot slide over each other. That is why an alloy is harder than the pure metal it is made from.
choices: A mixture of a metal with other elements|A pure metal|A metal compound|A metal that has been recycled
answer: A mixture of a metal with other elements

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Higher
ask: What is phytomining?
why: The ash is a concentrated ore. Bioleaching is the other biological method, using bacteria to produce a leachate. Both are slower than mining but work on ores too low in metal to be worth digging up.
choices: Growing plants that absorb metal compounds, then burning them to get the ore|Using bacteria to produce a metal solution|Mining metal from the sea bed|Extracting metal using electricity
answer: Growing plants that absorb metal compounds, then burning them to get the ore

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Higher
ask: Why is a low-carbon steel softer and more easily shaped than a high-carbon steel?
why: High-carbon steel is hard and brittle; low-carbon is soft and easily shaped. Same two elements, different proportions, opposite properties.
choices: Fewer carbon atoms disrupt the layers, so they slide more easily|It contains more iron atoms per gram|It has been heated for longer|It contains no impurities at all
answer: Fewer carbon atoms disrupt the layers, so they slide more easily

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the Haber process used to make?
why: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, at about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres and an iron catalyst. Nitrogen from the air, hydrogen from natural gas.
choices: Ammonia, for fertilisers|Sulfuric acid|Hydrogen, for fuel cells|Nitric acid

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Higher
ask: The Haber process runs at 450 °C although a lower temperature would give a higher yield. Why?
why: It is a compromise, and that word is the point of the question: the forward reaction is exothermic, so cooling improves the yield and ruins the rate. 450 °C is a deliberate trade between the two, with the unreacted gases recycled.
choices: A lower temperature would make the reaction far too slow|A lower temperature would damage the catalyst|The yield is actually higher at 450 °C|The nitrogen would liquefy
answer: A lower temperature would make the reaction far too slow

subject: Chemistry
name: Using Resources — GCSE Higher
ask: An NPK fertiliser supplies which three elements?
why: They are the three elements plants take from soil in the largest amounts, and the ones a crop removes when it is harvested. N, P and K are their symbols.
choices: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium|Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium carbonate|Nitrate, potassium and calcium|Nitrogen, potassium and calcium

subject: Physics
name: Energy — KS3
ask: Which energy store does a stretched spring have?
why: Stretching or squashing something springy stores energy in the elastic potential store, and it is returned when the spring goes back to its original shape.
choices: Elastic potential|Kinetic|Chemical|Thermal

subject: Physics
name: Energy — KS3
ask: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only...
why: That is conservation of energy. It is never used up — it ends up somewhere, usually spread out as heat in the surroundings, where it is much harder to use.
accept: transferred|transfered|moved|transferred from one store to another|changed|transferred between stores|stored|dissipated

subject: Physics
name: Energy — KS3
ask: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
why: Renewable means it is replenished as fast as it is used. Wind, solar, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal and biofuel are renewable; the fossil fuels and nuclear fuel are not.
choices: Wind|Coal|Natural gas|Nuclear fuel

subject: Physics
name: Energy — KS3
ask: How is energy transferred from a hot radiator to the air by conduction?
why: Conduction needs particles in contact, so it works best in solids. Convection is the moving fluid, and radiation is the only one that crosses empty space.
choices: Particles vibrate and pass energy to neighbouring particles|Warm air rises and cool air sinks|Infrared radiation travels across a vacuum|The radiator gives off light
answer: Particles vibrate and pass energy to neighbouring particles

subject: Physics
name: Energy — KS3
ask: Why does loft insulation reduce heat loss from a house?
why: Air conducts badly, and trapping it stops convection currents carrying the energy away. Most insulation works this way, including double glazing and a woolly jumper.
choices: It traps air, which is a poor conductor|It reflects all the heat back|It is very heavy|It absorbs the heat permanently
answer: It traps air, which is a poor conductor

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Foundation
ask: A 2 kg object moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
why: E = ½mv² = 0.5 × 2 × 3² = 0.5 × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Forgetting the half gives 18, and squaring after multiplying gives something else again — square the speed first.

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Foundation
ask: A 5 kg mass is lifted 2 m. What is the gain in gravitational potential energy? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
why: E = mgh = 5 × 9.8 × 2 = 98 J. The height is the VERTICAL distance — the length of a ramp is not h.

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Foundation
ask: A device takes in 200 J and usefully transfers 150 J. What is its efficiency?
why: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, so 75%. Over 100% means the division is upside down, which is the commonest slip here.

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the unit of power?
why: Power is energy transferred per second, so one watt is one joule per second. The joule is the energy itself.
choices: Watt|Joule|Newton|Volt

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Foundation
ask: Name one way energy is wasted in a moving machine.
why: Friction and air resistance both heat the surroundings, and some energy goes as sound. Lubrication and streamlining reduce them — you cannot remove them.
accept: friction|heating by friction|heat|thermal energy|air resistance|drag|sound|heating due to friction|resistance

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Higher
ask: A 0.5 kg ball falls 20 m. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
why: All the gravitational store becomes kinetic, so mgh = ½mv² and the mass cancels: v² = 2gh = 2 × 9.8 × 20 = 392, so v = √392 = 19.8 m/s. Forgetting the square root gives 392.

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Higher
ask: What is specific heat capacity?
why: E = mcΔθ. Water’s is unusually high at 4200 J/kg°C, which is why it is used in heating systems and why the sea warms so slowly.
choices: The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C|The energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance|The energy stored in 1 kg of a substance|The temperature a substance reaches when heated
answer: The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Higher
ask: How much energy raises 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg°C)
why: E = mcΔθ = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J. Δθ is the CHANGE in temperature, not the final temperature.

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Higher
ask: What is specific latent heat?
why: During melting or boiling the temperature holds flat, because the energy is breaking the forces between particles rather than making them move faster. That flat section on a heating graph is the latent heat being supplied.
choices: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change|The energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C|The energy lost by 1 kg as it cools|The energy stored in a hot object
answer: The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change

subject: Physics
name: Energy — GCSE Higher
ask: A motor transfers 600 J in 5 s. What is its power?
why: P = E ÷ t = 600 ÷ 5 = 120 W. Multiplying gives 3000, which would be an enormous power for a small motor — a sanity check catches it.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — KS3
ask: What does an ammeter measure?
why: An ammeter goes IN SERIES, because the current has to flow through it. A voltmeter goes in parallel, across the component.
choices: Current|Voltage|Resistance|Power

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — KS3
ask: In a series circuit with two identical bulbs, what happens if one bulb is removed?
why: A series circuit is one loop, so a break anywhere stops the current everywhere. In parallel each bulb has its own path, so the others keep working.
choices: The other goes out too|The other gets brighter|The other stays the same|The other flickers

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — KS3
ask: What is the unit of current?
why: Current is the rate of flow of charge — one amp is one coulomb of charge passing per second.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — KS3
ask: Which material is a good conductor of electricity?
why: Metals have free electrons that can move through the structure, which is what a current is. Plastic, rubber and glass hold their electrons in place, so they are insulators — which is why wire is copper inside and plastic outside.
choices: Copper|Plastic|Rubber|Glass

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — KS3
ask: What does a fuse do?
why: A thin wire that melts first is a deliberate weak point, so a fault cannot heat the cable enough to start a fire. A circuit breaker does the same job and can be reset.
choices: Melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too high|Increases the current in a circuit|Stores charge for later|Measures the voltage
answer: Melts and breaks the circuit if the current is too high

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Foundation
ask: A 12 V supply drives 3 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?
why: V = IR, so R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω. Multiplying gives 36, which is the commonest slip on this triangle.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Foundation
ask: In a SERIES circuit, the current...
why: There is only one path, so the same charge passes every point. It is the potential difference that is shared out in series — and in parallel it is the other way round.
choices: is the same everywhere|splits between the components|is largest near the battery|increases at each resistor

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Foundation
ask: Two 6 Ω resistors are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
why: In series resistances simply add. In parallel the total is LESS than either one, because adding another path makes it easier for charge to flow.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Foundation
ask: What happens to the resistance of a thermistor as it gets hotter?
why: That is what makes a thermistor useful in a thermostat — the current rises as it warms. An LDR does the same with light: brighter means lower resistance.
choices: It decreases|It increases|It stays the same|It becomes zero

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which wire in a UK plug is brown?
why: Brown live, blue neutral, green-and-yellow earth. The live carries the alternating potential difference from the supply, which is why it is the dangerous one even when a switch is off.
choices: Live|Neutral|Earth|Fuse wire

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Higher
ask: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. How much energy does it use in kWh?
why: E = P × t with power in kW and time in hours: 2 × 3 = 6 kWh. A kilowatt-hour is a unit of ENERGY, not power, which is why the electricity bill is in them.
choices: 6 kWh|0.67 kWh|600 kWh|5 kWh

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Higher
ask: Charge of 30 C flows in 10 s. What is the current?
why: Q = It, so I = Q ÷ t = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 A. One amp is one coulomb per second, which is the definition this rearrangement comes from.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the power of a device with a current of 4 A and a p.d. of 230 V?
why: P = VI = 230 × 4 = 920 W. P = I²R and P = V²/R are the other two forms, used when you know the resistance instead.

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Higher
ask: Why is the National Grid transmitted at very high potential difference?
why: For a given power, P = VI means raising V lowers I — and the heating loss is I²R, so halving the current quarters the loss. Step-up transformers at the station, step-down ones before homes.
choices: To lower the current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables|To make the electricity travel faster|To increase the current so more power arrives|To reduce the voltage at the power station
answer: To lower the current, so less energy is wasted heating the cables

subject: Physics
name: Electricity — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a wire get hot when a current flows through it?
why: More vibration is a higher temperature. It is a waste in a cable and the whole point in a kettle or a filament lamp — the same physics, wanted or not.
choices: Electrons collide with the ions in the wire, making them vibrate more|The electrons rub against the insulation|The voltage heats the wire directly|The wire expands and releases energy
answer: Electrons collide with the ions in the wire, making them vibrate more

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — KS3
ask: In which state are the particles furthest apart?
why: Gas particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, which is why a gas fills its container and can be compressed. Solids and liquids are both close-packed.
choices: Gas|Liquid|Solid|They are all the same

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — KS3
ask: What is density?
why: ρ = m/V. It is how much mass is packed into a given space, which is why a small dense object can outweigh a large light one.
choices: Mass divided by volume|Volume divided by mass|Mass multiplied by volume|Weight divided by area

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — KS3
ask: Why does a gas exert pressure on its container?
why: Each collision is a tiny force; billions of them add up to a steady push. Heat the gas and the particles hit harder and more often, so the pressure rises.
choices: Its particles collide with the walls|Its particles are attracted to the walls|The gas is heavier than air|The particles stick to each other
answer: Its particles collide with the walls

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — KS3
ask: What happens to the mass of a substance when it melts?
why: A change of state is a physical change — the same particles, rearranged. Nothing is added or removed, so the mass is conserved.
choices: It stays the same|It increases|It decreases|It doubles

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — KS3
ask: What is the name for a gas turning directly into a solid?
why: Sublimation is used for both directions of the solid-gas change, skipping the liquid entirely. Dry ice does it at ordinary pressure.
choices: Sublimation|Evaporation|Condensation|Melting

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Foundation
ask: An object has a mass of 300 g and a volume of 100 cm³. What is its density?
why: ρ = m ÷ V = 300 ÷ 100 = 3 g/cm³. Mass on top, always — dividing the other way gives 0.33 and a unit nobody uses.
choices: 3 g/cm³|0.33 g/cm³|30 000 g/cm³|200 g/cm³

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is a change of state a physical change?
why: Freeze water and you get the same water back. A chemical change makes something new, which is usually much harder to reverse.
choices: The substance can be changed back and keeps the same mass|A new substance is formed|It needs no energy|The particles are destroyed
answer: The substance can be changed back and keeps the same mass

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Foundation
ask: On a heating graph, what is happening during a flat section?
why: Energy is still going in, but it is breaking the forces between particles rather than making them move faster — so the temperature does not rise until the change is complete.
choices: The substance is changing state|The substance is cooling|Nothing is being heated|The thermometer is broken

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Foundation
ask: What happens to the pressure of a fixed volume of gas when it is heated?
why: Hotter particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder. A sealed can on a fire is exactly this, which is why the label says not to.
choices: It increases|It decreases|It stays the same|It becomes zero

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Foundation
ask: How would you measure the volume of an irregular solid?
why: The object pushes aside its own volume of water, so the rise in the reading IS the volume. A ruler only works on a regular shape.
choices: By displacement, using a measuring cylinder of water|With a ruler|By weighing it|By heating it until it melts
answer: By displacement, using a measuring cylinder of water

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Higher
ask: How much energy is needed to melt 2 kg of ice? (specific latent heat of fusion = 334 000 J/kg)
why: E = mL = 2 × 334 000 = 668 000 J. There is no Δθ in this formula, because the temperature does not change during melting.

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does the internal energy of a substance rise when it is heated but the temperature does not, during boiling?
why: Internal energy is kinetic plus potential. Temperature measures the KINETIC part only, so energy going into the potential part is invisible on a thermometer.
choices: The potential energy of the particles rises as the forces between them are broken|The kinetic energy of the particles rises|The mass of the substance increases|The particles get bigger
answer: The potential energy of the particles rises as the forces between them are broken

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Higher
ask: A gas is compressed quickly. What happens to its temperature and why?
why: Doing work transfers energy just as heating does, so the internal energy goes up. It is why a bicycle pump gets warm — nothing has been heated from outside.
choices: It rises, because work is done on the gas|It falls, because the volume is smaller|It stays the same, because no heat is added|It falls, because the particles have less room
answer: It rises, because work is done on the gas

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does increasing the volume of a gas at constant temperature lower its pressure?
why: Constant temperature means the SPEED is unchanged — only the frequency of collisions falls, because there is further to travel between walls. pV is constant.
choices: The particles hit the walls less often|The particles move more slowly|There are fewer particles|The particles become heavier
answer: The particles hit the walls less often

subject: Physics
name: Particle Model of Matter — GCSE Higher
ask: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
why: It is a property the system HAS. Heating and doing work are two ways of changing it — they are transfers, not stores.
choices: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles|The heat supplied to it|Its temperature|The work done on it
answer: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles

subject: Physics
name: Forces — KS3
ask: What is the unit of force?
why: One newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared. Mass is in kilograms; weight, which is a force, is in newtons.
choices: Newton|Joule|Watt|Kilogram

subject: Physics
name: Forces — KS3
ask: Which of these is a contact force?
why: A contact force needs the objects to touch — friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force. Gravity, magnetism and electrostatic forces all act at a distance.
choices: Friction|Gravity|Magnetism|Electrostatic force

subject: Physics
name: Forces — KS3
ask: A book rests on a table and does not move. What can you say about the forces on it?
why: Weight down, normal contact force up, equal in size. Balanced forces mean no change in motion — which includes staying still.
choices: They are balanced|There are no forces on it|Gravity is the only force|They are unbalanced upwards

subject: Physics
name: Forces — KS3
ask: What is the weight of a 10 kg mass on Earth? (g = 10 N/kg)
why: W = mg = 10 × 10 = 100 N. The mass would be 10 kg on the Moon too; the weight would be about 16 N, because g there is smaller.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — KS3
ask: A force is a vector. What does that mean?
why: Distance and speed are scalars — size only. Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors, which is why they are drawn as arrows.
choices: It has both size and direction|It can only be positive|It is measured in newtons|It acts at a distance
answer: It has both size and direction

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Foundation
ask: A 4 kg mass accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the resultant force?
why: F = ma = 4 × 3 = 12 N. Divide instead and the answer is smaller than either number, which is a quick sign it is wrong.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Foundation
ask: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph represent?
why: Distance ÷ time IS speed, and that is what a gradient is. On a VELOCITY-time graph the gradient is acceleration and the area is distance — two different graphs, two different meanings.
choices: Speed|Acceleration|Distance|Force

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is terminal velocity?
why: Air resistance grows with speed, so a falling object reaches a speed where the two forces balance. Balanced forces mean no acceleration — so it keeps falling, at a constant speed.
choices: The steady speed reached when air resistance equals weight|The fastest an object can ever go|The speed at which an object hits the ground|The speed at the start of a fall
answer: The steady speed reached when air resistance equals weight

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Foundation
ask: How much work is done lifting a 20 N weight through 3 m?
why: W = Fs = 20 × 3 = 60 J. Work done is energy transferred, which is why both are measured in joules.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Foundation
ask: A spring extends 4 cm under a force of 8 N. What is the spring constant in N/m?
why: F = ke, so k = F ÷ e — but e must be in METRES: 4 cm = 0.04 m, and 8 ÷ 0.04 = 200 N/m. Leaving it in centimetres gives 2, which is the trap.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the momentum of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s?
why: p = mv = 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s. Momentum is a vector, so direction matters when two objects collide.
choices: 30 000 kg m/s|75 kg m/s|1520 kg m/s|300 000 kg m/s

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a crumple zone reduce the force in a crash?
why: F = Δp/Δt. The change in momentum is fixed — the car is stopping either way — so the only thing that can be changed is the time. Airbags, seatbelts and crash mats all do the same thing.
choices: It increases the time taken to stop, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller|It reduces the mass of the car|It reduces the momentum before the crash|It makes the car stop faster
answer: It increases the time taken to stop, so the rate of change of momentum is smaller

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Higher
ask: An object accelerates from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
why: a = Δv ÷ t = (15 − 5) ÷ 4 = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 m/s². Using the final velocity instead of the change gives 3.75.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Higher
ask: Using v² − u² = 2as, what is the final speed of an object starting from rest and accelerating at 4 m/s² over 8 m?
why: u = 0, so v² = 2 × 4 × 8 = 64, and v = √64 = 8 m/s. Missing the square root gives 64.

subject: Physics
name: Forces — GCSE Higher
ask: What does Newton’s third law say?
why: The two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, which is why they do not cancel out. If they acted on the same one nothing could ever accelerate.
choices: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, on a different object|A resultant force causes acceleration|An object stays still unless a force acts|Momentum is always conserved
answer: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, on a different object

subject: Physics
name: Waves — KS3
ask: What is the wavelength of a wave?
why: Wavelength is a distance, measured in metres. The height is the amplitude and the number per second is the frequency — three different measurements of one wave.
choices: The distance from one peak to the next|The height of a peak|The number of waves per second|The speed of the wave
answer: The distance from one peak to the next

subject: Physics
name: Waves — KS3
ask: Sound is which type of wave?
why: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction the wave travels, making compressions and rarefactions. That is also why sound needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum.
choices: Longitudinal|Transverse|Electromagnetic|It is not a wave

subject: Physics
name: Waves — KS3
ask: What is the unit of frequency?
why: One hertz is one wave per second. A 50 Hz mains supply changes direction fifty times a second.

subject: Physics
name: Waves — KS3
ask: What happens to light when it passes from air into glass?
why: That is refraction. The bending happens because one side of the beam enters the denser material first and slows before the other — which is also why a beam hitting head-on does not bend at all.
choices: It slows down and changes direction|It speeds up|It stops|It changes colour
answer: It slows down and changes direction

subject: Physics
name: Waves — KS3
ask: What does the law of reflection say?
why: Both angles are measured from the NORMAL — the line at right angles to the surface — not from the surface itself.
choices: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection|The angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection|Light always reflects straight back|The angle depends on the colour
answer: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. What is its speed?
why: v = fλ = 50 × 4 = 200 m/s. Dividing gives 12.5, which is the slip to watch for.

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which of these is a transverse wave?
why: In a transverse wave the vibration is at right angles to the travel. Water waves and all electromagnetic waves are transverse; sound and ultrasound are longitudinal.
choices: A water wave|A sound wave|An ultrasound wave|A wave on a slinky being pushed

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the amplitude of a wave?
why: From the middle to a peak, not from trough to peak — that measurement is twice the amplitude. Larger amplitude means a louder sound or a brighter light.
choices: The maximum displacement from the rest position|The distance between two peaks|The number of waves per second|The total height from trough to peak
answer: The maximum displacement from the rest position

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: A wave has a period of 0.2 s. What is its frequency?
why: f = 1 ÷ T = 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 Hz. Period and frequency are reciprocals — one is seconds per wave and the other is waves per second.
choices: 5 Hz|0.2 Hz|20 Hz|0.8 Hz

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: Waves transfer energy without transferring what?
why: A float on a pond bobs up and down but does not travel with the wave. The particles oscillate about a fixed position; only the energy moves along.

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Sound travels at 340 m/s. What is the wavelength of a 170 Hz note?
why: λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 170 = 2 m. Multiplying gives 57 800 m, which is plainly not a sound wavelength — a sanity check catches it.

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: What happens to a wave that meets a boundary at an angle and enters a slower medium?
why: Slower means towards the normal; faster means away. Slowing down on entering water or glass is why a straw looks bent.
choices: It refracts towards the normal|It refracts away from the normal|It is always totally reflected|It continues in a straight line

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Why can ultrasound be used to see inside the body?
why: The time each echo takes to return gives the depth of that boundary. It is non-ionising, which is why it is used on a foetus where X-rays would not be.
choices: It partly reflects at each boundary between different tissues|It passes straight through every tissue|It is absorbed by bone only|It ionises the tissue
answer: It partly reflects at each boundary between different tissues

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Which electromagnetic waves are most dangerous because they are ionising?
why: They are the highest-frequency end of the spectrum, so they carry the most energy per photon — enough to knock electrons off atoms and damage DNA.
choices: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays|Radio waves and microwaves|Infrared and visible light|Microwaves only

subject: Physics
name: Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Put these in order of INCREASING wavelength: X-rays, radio waves, visible light.
why: The spectrum runs radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma — wavelength falling and frequency rising along it. Increasing wavelength is that list read backwards.
choices: X-rays, visible light, radio waves|Radio waves, visible light, X-rays|Visible light, X-rays, radio waves|X-rays, radio waves, visible light

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — KS3
ask: What is at the centre of an atom?
why: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, and is about 1/10000 of the size of the atom. The electrons occupy the rest.
choices: The nucleus|An electron shell|A neutron only|Empty space

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — KS3
ask: What is radioactive decay?
why: It is random — nothing makes a particular nucleus decay at a particular moment, and nothing outside it can speed it up or slow it down.
choices: An unstable nucleus giving out radiation to become more stable|An atom losing an electron|An atom being split by a scientist|A chemical reaction inside an atom
answer: An unstable nucleus giving out radiation to become more stable

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — KS3
ask: Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
why: Alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, gamma only reduced by thick lead or concrete. Alpha is the most ionising, which is exactly why it does not get far.
choices: Alpha|Beta|Gamma|None of them

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — KS3
ask: What is an alpha particle made of?
why: It is a helium nucleus. Beta is a fast electron from the nucleus, and gamma is an electromagnetic wave with no mass and no charge.
choices: Two protons and two neutrons|One electron|A high-energy wave|One proton

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — KS3
ask: Name one source of background radiation.
why: Background radiation is around us all the time — mostly natural, from radon in rocks, cosmic rays and even food. It is why a measurement must have the background subtracted.
accept: radon|radon gas|rocks|the ground|soil|cosmic rays|space|the sun|food|medical x-rays|x-rays|buildings|nuclear waste|air travel

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is half-life?
why: It can also be defined as the time for the count rate to fall by half. Because it is always a halving, a sample never reaches zero — it just becomes very small.
choices: The time for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay|The time for a sample to become completely safe|Half the time a sample lasts|The time for the mass to halve
answer: The time for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: A sample has a count rate of 800 and a half-life of 2 days. What is the count rate after 6 days?
why: 6 days is three half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100. Dividing by three rather than halving three times gives 267, which is the commonest wrong route.

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, what happens to its mass number?
why: An alpha is two protons and two neutrons, so the mass number drops by 4 and the atomic number by 2. Beta decay is different — mass unchanged, atomic number up by 1.
choices: It falls by 4|It falls by 2|It stays the same|It rises by 4

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which type of radiation is the most penetrating?
why: Penetration and ionising power run opposite ways: gamma ionises least, so it passes through most. Alpha ionises most and is stopped almost at once.
choices: Gamma|Alpha|Beta|They are equal

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Foundation
ask: Why is a source with a long half-life a problem as waste?
why: Long half-life means low activity but for centuries; short half-life means high activity that fades fast. Which is more dangerous depends entirely on whether it is inside you.
choices: It stays radioactive for a very long time and must be stored safely|It gives out much more radiation each second|It becomes more radioactive over time|It cannot be detected
answer: It stays radioactive for a very long time and must be stored safely

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: What is nuclear fission?
why: It usually needs a neutron to be absorbed first, and releases two or three more — which is the chain reaction. Fusion is the opposite and is what powers stars.
choices: A large unstable nucleus splitting into two smaller ones|Two small nuclei joining together|A nucleus emitting an alpha particle|An electron being knocked off an atom
answer: A large unstable nucleus splitting into two smaller ones

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: What do control rods do in a nuclear reactor?
why: Fewer neutrons means fewer fissions. The moderator is the different job — slowing neutrons so they are absorbed rather than passing through.
choices: Absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction|Slow the neutrons down so fission is more likely|Carry heat away to the boiler|Shield the workers from gamma rays
answer: Absorb neutrons to control the rate of the chain reaction

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures and pressures?
why: Both nuclei are positive and repel hard at close range. Only at enormous speed do they get near enough for the strong nuclear force to take over — which is why fusion happens in stars and is so difficult on Earth.
choices: To overcome the electrostatic repulsion between two positive nuclei|To break the nuclei into smaller pieces|To turn the fuel into a liquid|To produce enough neutrons
answer: To overcome the electrostatic repulsion between two positive nuclei

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: A sample falls from 1600 counts/s to 200 counts/s in 12 hours. What is the half-life?
why: 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 is three halvings, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 hours. Count the halvings first, then divide the time by that number.
choices: 4 hours|3 hours|6 hours|1.5 hours

subject: Physics
name: Atomic Structure — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
why: An irradiated object does not become radioactive and the exposure stops when the source is removed. Contamination travels with you and keeps decaying, which is why it is the harder problem.
choices: Contamination is radioactive material getting on or in you; irradiation is being exposed to the radiation|They are the same thing|Contamination is being exposed; irradiation is material getting on you|Contamination only happens with gamma rays
answer: Contamination is radioactive material getting on or in you; irradiation is being exposed to the radiation

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — KS3
ask: What happens when two north poles are brought together?
why: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Repulsion is the only sure test for a magnet, because a magnet will attract an unmagnetised piece of iron too.
choices: They repel|They attract|Nothing happens|They become south poles

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — KS3
ask: Which of these materials is magnetic?
why: Iron, cobalt, nickel and steel are magnetic. Copper and aluminium are metals and conduct electricity well, but a magnet does not attract them.
choices: Iron|Copper|Aluminium|Plastic

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — KS3
ask: How could you make an electromagnet stronger?
why: More turns, more current, or an iron core — all three strengthen it. The great advantage over a permanent magnet is that it can be switched off, which is what a scrapyard crane needs.
choices: Add more turns of wire to the coil|Use a thinner wire|Reduce the current|Use a plastic core
answer: Add more turns of wire to the coil

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — KS3
ask: Which way does a compass needle point?
why: A compass needle is a small magnet free to turn, so it lines up with the Earth’s field — which is evidence that the Earth’s core is magnetic.
choices: To the Earth’s magnetic north|Straight down|Towards the Sun|Towards the nearest metal

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — KS3
ask: Where is a magnet’s field strongest?
why: On a field diagram the lines are closest together at the poles, and how close the lines are is exactly what shows the strength.
choices: At the poles|In the middle|All over equally|Just outside the poles

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which way do magnetic field lines point?
why: Outside the magnet they run north to south; inside they complete the loop the other way. The direction is the way the north pole of a compass would point.
choices: From north to south outside the magnet|From south to north outside the magnet|Always towards the magnet|Always away from the magnet
answer: From north to south outside the magnet

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is induced magnetism?
why: Induced magnetism is always attraction, and it disappears when the field is removed — which is why a paper clip falls off as soon as the magnet is taken away.
choices: A magnetic material becoming a magnet when placed in a magnetic field|A magnet losing its magnetism when heated|A current being produced by a moving magnet|A magnet made by stroking with another magnet
answer: A magnetic material becoming a magnet when placed in a magnetic field

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?
why: Permanent means its own field, always. Induced means borrowed from a nearby field and lost when that field goes.
choices: A permanent magnet produces its own field all the time|An induced magnet is always stronger|A permanent magnet can be switched off|An induced magnet is made of copper
answer: A permanent magnet produces its own field all the time

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Foundation
ask: What does the motor effect describe?
why: The wire’s own field interacts with the magnet’s. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the direction — first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion.
choices: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force|A moving magnet produces a current in a wire|A magnet attracts iron filings|A current makes a wire hot
answer: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Foundation
ask: Around a straight wire carrying a current, the magnetic field is...
why: The circles get further apart with distance, so the field weakens. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.
choices: a series of concentric circles|straight lines along the wire|a single loop|the same shape as a bar magnet’s

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Higher
ask: What is the generator effect?
why: It is the motor effect run backwards: motion in, electricity out. Either the conductor moves or the field changes — what matters is that the field through the circuit is changing.
choices: A potential difference is induced when a conductor moves through a magnetic field|A wire carrying a current experiences a force|A magnet attracts a piece of iron|A current makes a coil into a magnet
answer: A potential difference is induced when a conductor moves through a magnetic field

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Higher
ask: Calculate the force on a 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A in a 0.4 T field, at right angles. (F = BIl)
why: F = BIl = 0.4 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.6 N. At right angles is required — a wire parallel to the field feels no force at all.

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Higher
ask: A step-up transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 500 on the secondary. The input is 20 V. What is the output?
why: Vₛ/Vₚ = nₛ/nₚ, so Vₛ = 20 × 500/100 = 100 V. More turns on the secondary means a higher voltage — which is what step-up means, so an answer below 20 V is the ratio inverted.

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Higher
ask: A transformer is 100% efficient. What does that tell you about the power?
why: VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ. That is why the National Grid can transmit at very high voltage and low current, wasting far less energy in the cables.
choices: The power in equals the power out, so raising V lowers I|The current is the same on both sides|The voltage is the same on both sides|No energy is transferred
answer: The power in equals the power out, so raising V lowers I

subject: Physics
name: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does a transformer not work with direct current?
why: Induction depends on the field through the secondary CHANGING. Alternating current reverses fifty times a second, so the field is never still.
choices: A steady current gives a steady field, and only a CHANGING field induces a p.d.|Direct current is too weak|The iron core only works with a.c.|Direct current cannot flow in a coil
answer: A steady current gives a steady field, and only a CHANGING field induces a p.d.

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — KS3
ask: Which of these can travel through a vacuum?
why: Electromagnetic waves need no medium, which is why we can see the Sun. Sound needs particles to vibrate, so space is silent.
choices: Light|Sound|Both equally|Neither

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — KS3
ask: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum can we see?
why: Visible light is a very narrow band in the middle of the spectrum. Everything either side of it is real radiation we cannot see, which is why detectors are needed.
choices: Visible light|Infrared|Ultraviolet|Microwaves

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — KS3
ask: What are microwaves used for?
why: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules in food, heating it from within, and they also pass through the atmosphere well — which is what makes them good for satellites.
choices: Cooking and satellite communication|Taking pictures of bones|Sterilising surgical instruments|Suntanning beds

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — KS3
ask: Which radiation do we feel as heat from a fire?
why: Every object emits infrared, and the hotter it is the more it emits. Thermal imaging cameras detect exactly this.

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — KS3
ask: Why should you wear sunscreen?
why: Ultraviolet is ionising, so it can damage DNA and cause skin cancer. It is the high-frequency end of the spectrum where the danger starts.
choices: It absorbs ultraviolet, which can damage skin cells|It reflects all visible light|It blocks infrared so you stay cool|It stops X-rays from the Sun
answer: It absorbs ultraviolet, which can damage skin cells

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. What speed?
why: Three hundred million metres per second. 340 m/s is the speed of sound in air, which is nearly a million times slower — hence the gap between lightning and thunder.

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: What are radio waves mainly used for?
why: They have the longest wavelength, so they diffract around hills and buildings and travel a long way — which is what a broadcast needs.
choices: Television and radio broadcasting|Cooking food|Medical imaging of bones|Detecting forged banknotes

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which electromagnetic wave is used to check for broken bones?
why: X-rays pass through soft tissue and are absorbed by bone, so the bone shows as a shadow. They are ionising, which is why exposure is kept as low as possible.
choices: X-rays|Radio waves|Infrared|Microwaves

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: What happens when an object absorbs electromagnetic radiation?
why: Absorbed energy has to go somewhere. Emission is the reverse — a hot object gives out radiation, which is why a good absorber is also a good emitter.
choices: Its energy increases, often warming it|It reflects the same radiation back|It becomes radioactive|Its mass increases
answer: Its energy increases, often warming it

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which colour of surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation?
why: Matt black absorbs best and also emits best; shiny silver reflects and emits least. That is why a solar panel is black and a survival blanket is silver.
choices: Matt black|Shiny silver|Shiny white|Matt white

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: What produces gamma rays?
why: Gamma comes from the nucleus; X-rays come from electrons being stopped suddenly. They overlap in wavelength, so it is the ORIGIN that tells them apart, not the frequency.
choices: Changes in the nucleus of an atom|Electrons moving between energy levels|A heated filament|An oscillating electrical circuit
answer: Changes in the nucleus of an atom

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Why do radio waves diffract around hills more than visible light does?
