why: Diffraction is greatest when the wavelength and the gap or obstacle are comparable. Light’s wavelength is under a micrometre, so a hill is billions of times too big for it to bend around.
choices: Their wavelength is similar to the size of the obstacle|They travel faster|They carry more energy|They are longitudinal
answer: Their wavelength is similar to the size of the obstacle

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: An object is in thermal equilibrium. What does that mean about its radiation?
why: Its temperature stays constant because the two rates match. If absorption exceeds emission it warms — which is the whole mechanism of the greenhouse effect.
choices: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it|It absorbs no radiation at all|It emits no radiation at all|It only reflects radiation
answer: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: What happens to the intensity and wavelength of radiation emitted by an object as it gets hotter?
why: It is why metal glows red, then orange, then white as it heats — the peak is climbing from infrared into and through the visible range.
choices: Intensity rises and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths|Intensity rises and the peak moves to longer wavelengths|Intensity falls and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths|Neither changes
answer: Intensity rises and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths

subject: Physics
name: Electromagnetic Waves — GCSE Higher
ask: Ultraviolet is used in security marking because...
why: Fluorescence absorbs ultraviolet and re-emits visible light. The same effect makes a white shirt glow under a nightclub lamp.
choices: special ink fluoresces under UV but is invisible in ordinary light|UV burns a mark into the surface|UV passes through metal|UV is the only radiation that reflects off ink
answer: special ink fluoresces under UV but is invisible in ordinary light

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — KS3
ask: What is at the centre of our Solar System?
why: The planets orbit the Sun because of its gravity. The Moon orbits the Earth — a natural satellite of a planet rather than of the star.
choices: The Sun|The Earth|The Moon|A black hole

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — KS3
ask: What keeps a planet in orbit around the Sun?
why: Gravity pulls the planet towards the Sun while it moves sideways fast enough to keep missing. That constant change of direction is what an orbit is.
choices: Gravity|Magnetism|Air resistance|The solar wind

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — KS3
ask: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
why: One orbit is a year; one spin on its axis is a day. The Moon takes about a month to go round the Earth.
choices: One year|One day|One month|Ten years

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — KS3
ask: What is a galaxy?
why: Our galaxy is the Milky Way, and the Sun is one ordinary star in it. There are billions of galaxies in the observable universe.
choices: A huge collection of billions of stars|A planet with rings|A group of eight planets|A very large star
answer: A huge collection of billions of stars

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — KS3
ask: Why can we see the Moon?
why: The Moon is a cold rock. The phases are just how much of its sunlit half we can see from where we are.
choices: It reflects light from the Sun|It produces its own light|It burns hydrogen|It glows from heat
answer: It reflects light from the Sun

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Foundation
ask: What force causes a cloud of dust and gas to form a star?
why: Gravity pulls the nebula together, and the compression heats it. When it is hot enough, hydrogen nuclei fuse — and the star is born.
choices: Gravity|The strong nuclear force|Magnetism|Electrostatic attraction

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Foundation
ask: What is the main sequence stage of a star?
why: Two opposing effects hold it steady, which is why it lasts billions of years. The star changes only when the hydrogen begins to run out and the balance fails.
choices: A long stable period where gravity is balanced by outward pressure from fusion|The stage just before a star forms|The final stage of a very large star|The stage when a star becomes a black hole
answer: A long stable period where gravity is balanced by outward pressure from fusion

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Foundation
ask: What will our Sun become after the red giant stage?
why: A star of our Sun’s size sheds its outer layers and the core shrinks to a white dwarf. Only much more massive stars explode as supernovae and leave a neutron star or a black hole.
choices: A white dwarf|A neutron star|A black hole|A supernova

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Foundation
ask: What does red-shift tell us about distant galaxies?
why: The light is stretched to longer wavelengths, which is towards the red end. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes — the evidence the universe is expanding.
choices: They are moving away from us|They are moving towards us|They are made of red stars|They are very hot
answer: They are moving away from us

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Foundation
ask: Which theory is supported by red-shift and the cosmic microwave background?
why: Both fit a universe that began in a very small dense region and has been expanding ever since. The microwave background is the afterglow, stretched into the microwave range by that expansion.
accept: big bang|the big bang|big bang theory|the big bang theory|bigbang

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Higher
ask: Why does an object in a circular orbit accelerate even at constant speed?
why: Velocity is a vector, so changing direction IS changing velocity. Gravity provides the centripetal force, always at right angles to the motion — which turns it without speeding it up.
choices: Its direction, and so its velocity, is constantly changing|Its speed is secretly increasing|Gravity increases as it orbits|It is not accelerating
answer: Its direction, and so its velocity, is constantly changing

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Higher
ask: A satellite is moved to a higher orbit. What happens to its speed?
why: Gravity is weaker further out, so less centripetal force is available — and a slower speed is what that supports. That is also why higher orbits take longer.
choices: It must travel more slowly to stay in a stable orbit|It must travel faster|Its speed does not change|It cannot stay in orbit at all
answer: It must travel more slowly to stay in a stable orbit

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Higher
ask: How does a star of much greater mass than the Sun end its life?
why: The explosion is where elements heavier than iron are made and scattered — which is why there is iron in your blood and calcium in your bones.
choices: As a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole|As a white dwarf, then a black dwarf|By slowly cooling into a planet|By becoming a nebula only
answer: As a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Higher
ask: Where did elements heavier than iron come from?
why: Fusion in a star only builds up as far as iron, because beyond that it takes energy in rather than releasing it. Only the violence of a supernova supplies that energy.
choices: Supernova explosions|Fusion in main sequence stars|The Big Bang itself|Radioactive decay on planets

subject: Physics
name: Space Physics — GCSE Higher
ask: The Big Bang theory is supported by, among other things, the cosmic microwave background radiation. What is it?
why: It comes from every direction almost equally, which is hard to explain any other way. It was gamma and X-ray at the start and has been stretched into the microwave range by the expansion since.
choices: Radiation left over from the early universe, stretched by expansion|Radiation given off by the Milky Way|Microwaves reflected from distant galaxies|Heat from the Sun spread through space
answer: Radiation left over from the early universe, stretched by expansion
